prompt:
Name a key person in the humanist tradition and describe the approach taken by him/her to the human search for the meaning of life.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
One key person in the humanist tradition is Karl Marx (1818-1883). He was born in Trier in Germany and was more a political theorist than a philosopher. In London he met Friedrich Engels, who showed him the harsh conditions of English factory workers, and there he wrote his most famous work, Das Kapital.

Marx's approach to the search for meaning did not involve God. He rejected religion and believed that human reason and consciousness are what matter most. For Marx, meaning is found through work. The world is created by human work, and human labour creates history. A person's place in work and production decides their quality of life.

Marx said that most suffering comes from alienation. This happens when the masses work for little or no wage, while a few people control production and take most of the profit. Workers then feel powerless and as if they do not belong.

His answer was a fair society, based on people's abilities and needs, with shared ownership and shared responsibility. He believed people find happiness when the resources of society are shared equally among all. Through reason and the struggle for freedom, humans can be free to find meaning, and no one should be a slave to any system, whether work or religion.
marking_scheme: 20 marks, graded. Marking criteria: an excellent answer will show an understanding of a world view by accurately naming one key person in the humanist tradition and giving an accurate account of the approach taken by him/her to the search for the meaning of life. Possible points: e.g. Sartre - humans define and create ourselves by the choices we make; when faced with an absurd world people must create their own meaning of life. e.g. Marx - through using reason humans could be free to find meaning; people achieve happiness when the resources of society are shared equally amongst all the members. Other valid answers accepted. Graded: Excellent 20-17, Very Good 16-14, Good 13-11, Fair 10-8, Weak 7-5, then 4-2 and 1-0.

prompt:
Outline how the human search for the meaning of life can be seen in a sacred artefact associated with an ancient culture that you have studied.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Newgrange in County Meath is a sacred site built by Neolithic people around 3200 BCE. It shows their great skill and also a spiritual side to their lives.

The mound was used for burial and for rituals linked to the winter solstice. It is lined up with the movement of the sun. On 21 December, the shortest day of the year, the rising sun shines through the roof box above the entrance and lights up the inner chamber. After that date the days get longer. For these people the sun had returned and darkness was defeated. This may have given them hope at the darkest time of year, and hope in the face of death.

The stones are covered in carved Megalithic art, such as spirals and wavy lines, especially on the huge entrance stone. Some scholars think the spirals stand for the cycle of life, death and rebirth. Others think they stand for the sun, moon and stars.

This shows the search for meaning because the builders wanted to be in harmony with the universe. They seem to have sensed something 'other', even sacred, at the centre of life. Burying their dead in a place lit by the returning sun suggests they were asking what happens after death and hoping for new life.
marking_scheme: 20 marks, graded. Marking criteria: an excellent answer will show an understanding of the search for the meaning of life in an ancient society by setting out accurate information on how the search for the meaning of life can be seen in the way that an object, made by people in an ancient culture, was set apart for religious use. Possible points: e.g. Celtic artefacts decorated with birds may be associated with the belief that birds were spiritual messengers who brought communication from the spirit world. e.g. Newgrange, Co. Meath may suggest a belief in the cycle of life, death and rebirth; by aligning the burial mound to the sun at the winter solstice perhaps people were seeking hope that the sun would not be defeated by darkness and death. Note: if the object was made by people not associated with an ancient culture, the examiner consults the Advising Examiner. prompt:
Describe two examples of how the understanding of divine revelation in different major world religions is reflected in the way believers treat their sacred texts.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Divine revelation means God making himself known to people. Judaism, Christianity and Islam are called 'religions of the book' because they believe God's revelation is recorded in their sacred books.

Example 1: Christianity. Christians believe God revealed himself through the history of the Jewish people and, above all, in Jesus Christ. Jesus is the high point of revelation: 'The Word became flesh and lived among us' (John 1:14). His life, death and resurrection are God's most complete self-communication, and the Gospels record them. Because of this, Christians treat the Bible as the Word of God. At Mass, in the Liturgy of the Word, the readings are proclaimed as the word of God, and a Gospel reading is part of the ritual of each Sacrament. Christians also read and pray with the Bible to come to know Jesus. It is a source of comfort, challenge and inspiration. Tradition and the authority of the Christian community guide how the texts are interpreted, because Christians believe God is still revealing himself day by day.

Example 2: Islam. Muslims believe Allah revealed the Qur'an to the Prophet Muhammad through the archangel Gabriel (Jibril). It began in a cave on Mount Hira and went on bit by bit for about twenty-three years, until 632 CE. Muhammad is the Seal of the Prophets, so the Qur'an is the complete and final revelation. Muslims believe it does not just report what God said. It contains God's own words. Because of this, the Qur'an is treated with the greatest respect. It is not open to change or criticism, and it is kept in its original Arabic. Muslims see it as the only true source of knowledge of God and live by it every day, for example through the Five Pillars.

Marking criteria: an excellent answer will show an understanding of divine revelation by giving an accurate account of the way the will of God/gods/the divine made known in sacred texts is evident in how they are treated by believers in two major world religions. Possible points: Christianity e.g. the Gospels recognise the role of Jesus' life, death and resurrection in divine revelation; in the Liturgy of the Word the text is treated as the word of God. Islam e.g. Allah's revelation to Muhammad - the Qur'an. Other valid answers accepted. Marked as 20 marks x 2 (one 20-mark grade for each of the two parts). Each graded: Excellent 20-17, Very Good 16-14, Good 13-11, Fair 10-8, Weak 7-5, then 4-2 and 1-0.

topic_label: Modern and traditional images of God
prompt:
People express ideas about God in different ways:
- ART
- FILM
- MUSIC
Compare the understanding of God expressed in a modern image from one of the above with the understanding of God found in a long-established image from a major world religion.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Modern image (Music): 'You Say' by Lauren Daigle. Lauren Daigle is an American contemporary Christian singer-songwriter who mixes a modern style with Christian themes. Her song 'You Say' has had over 243 million views on YouTube. It is about identity: who we are in God's eyes, even when the world tells us otherwise. The understanding of God here is a God who is close and personal. God loves us, values us and gives us our true worth.

Long-established image (Christianity): God as Father. Jesus called God his father, using the close, loving word 'Abba'. In the prayer he taught his disciples he said, 'Father, hallowed be your name' (Luke 11:1-4). This image is also found in traditional art, such as 'God the Father' by Luca Cambiaso, and it is used in prayer and worship. It shows God caring for humanity as a parent cares for a child, protecting and guiding them.

Similarities: Both images show a God who cares deeply about each person. In both, our worth comes from our relationship with God. A loving father protects and guides his child. In the same way, the God of Daigle's song tells us who we really are when the world puts us down. Both also link to the image of God as Love, seen in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15).

Differences: The traditional Father image grew up in a patriarchal society. It is male and can suggest power and authority, like other traditional images such as the Creator and the all-powerful protector. The Catechism reminds us that God is neither man nor woman, so the image has limits. The modern song does not use a male picture of God at all. It stresses closeness, love and personal identity rather than power. It speaks to young people today who feel pressure about how they look and who they are. So the modern image brings out the loving, personal side of God, while the long-established image stresses God's fatherly care and authority.
marking_scheme: 40 marks, graded. Marking criteria: an excellent answer will show an understanding of images of God by giving an accurate account of a similarity and/or difference between the ideas about God expressed in a modern image from Art or Film or Music and the understanding of God found in a traditional image from one major world religion. Possible points: ART e.g. Janice McKenzie's 'Jesus of the People' - image of God as an African American woman is similar to a Jewish Biblical understanding of God as maternal, expressed in the image of God as a comforting mother (Isaiah). FILM e.g. 'Bruce Almighty' - image of God as omnipotent, omniscient and endowed with magical powers is similar to the traditional image of God as the supreme being/creator found in Genesis. MUSIC e.g. Kanye West's 'Jesus Walks' - image of God as one who cares for everyone is similar to the Gospel image of God caring for the marginalised and oppressed. Graded: Excellent 40-34, Very Good 33-28, Good 27-22, Fair 21-16, Weak 15-10, then 9-4 and 3-0.

prompt:
BUDDHISM / CHRISTIANITY / HINDUISM / ISLAM / JUDAISM
Profile the connection between the understanding of the transcendent/God and how the human person is understood in the teaching of two of the above world religions.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Judaism. In Judaism, God is understood above all as Creator and as Liberator. In Genesis 1, God creates humankind 'in his image... male and female he created them'. So Jewish people see each person as unique, set apart from the rest of creation and in a special relationship with God. Genesis 2-3 also tells of the 'fall', when humanity became estranged from God. So the person is both loved by God and distant from him. In the Exodus God frees his people from slavery and makes a covenant with them at Mount Sinai, giving the Ten Commandments. As a result, Jewish people see themselves as God's chosen people, liberated by God and called to be faithful in return. This shapes how they live: they keep the Sabbath to praise God the creator, they do not make images of God or say his name aloud, they keep the Law (for example, kosher food laws and the prayer shawl with 613 tassels), and they celebrate Passover to remember their liberation.

Christianity. Christians share the same creation accounts, so they also see God as creator and every person as made for a relationship with God. As St Augustine said, 'our hearts are restless until they find their rest in you.' Because God made the world good, humans are the high point of creation but also its stewards. They must care for the earth, as Pope Francis urges in Laudato si'. Christians also believe God is revealed in a unique way in Jesus Christ, 'the image of the invisible God' (Colossians 1:15). Jesus' death and resurrection show God's unconditional love. So Christians understand themselves as loved, forgiven and redeemed. This calls them to live by the law of love - love God and love your neighbour - and to be merciful and forgiving, as Martin Luther King and Mother Teresa were.

Marking criteria: an excellent answer will show an understanding of the religious values of major world religions by accurately tracing the relationship between the understanding of the transcendent/God and the understanding of the human person in the teaching of two of the listed world religions. Possible points: BUDDHISM - the transcendent is indefinable, non-personal, absolute; the person is marked by suffering caused by desire but can reach enlightenment and Nirvana through suppressing desire. CHRISTIANITY - God is creator; immanence and transcendence are fused in Jesus Christ, whose life, death and resurrection revealed God's unconditional love; the person is the high point of creation, made in the image and likeness of God. HINDUISM - Brahman is supreme creator made manifest in all creation; the goal of life is liberation and union with Brahman; following Dharma brings a better rebirth and closer to Moksha. ISLAM - Allah is one, all-powerful and merciful, communicating his will through Muhammad and the Qur'an; the person, created by God, has a duty to live by the Five Pillars. JUDAISM - God is all-powerful creator, a liberating God who cares for his people and enters a Covenant with them; humans have a moral and spiritual nature that finds fulfilment in God. prompt:
AN EVANGELIST (Matthew or Mark or Luke or John) / JOSEPHUS / PLINY THE YOUNGER / SAINT PAUL / TACITUS
Compare the importance of the writings of two of the above as sources of historical evidence for the existence of Jesus of Nazareth.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Tacitus (c. 56-117 CE) was a Roman historian writing around 115 CE. He mentions Jesus when writing about the burning of Rome in 64 CE, when Emperor Nero blamed the Christians. He wrote that 'Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of... Pontius Pilate'. He called Christianity a 'pernicious superstition' that spread from Judea to Rome. His writing confirms three things: Jesus existed, he was executed under Pontius Pilate, and his followers had reached Rome.

Josephus (c. 37-100 CE) was a Jewish historian who wrote The Jewish War and The Jewish Antiquities. He mentions Jesus near the end of his life, about sixty years after the crucifixion. He places Jesus at the centre of disturbances among the Jews when Pilate ruled (26-36 CE). He describes Jesus as 'a wise man, a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of men who receive the truth with pleasure.'

Similarities: Both are secular (non-religious) sources, not Christian faith documents. Both are secondary sources written decades after Jesus' death, which is normal for ancient history. There are no primary sources even for Socrates. Both link Jesus to the time of Pontius Pilate. Both are seen as authoritative because they were not followers of Jesus and had no reason to invent him.

Differences: Tacitus was openly hostile to Christians, so the fact that he still accepts that Jesus existed makes his evidence very strong. Josephus writes much more favourably. He accepts both that Jesus was real and that he had a deep and lasting impact on the people he met. Tacitus, a Roman, tells us mainly about Jesus' death and the spread of Christianity to Rome. Josephus, a Jew, tells us more about Jesus' character and work in Palestine.

So together they give strong outside evidence, from both a Roman and a Jewish writer, that Jesus of Nazareth really lived.
marking_scheme: 40 marks, graded. Marking criteria: an excellent answer will show knowledge of the sources of evidence for Jesus of Nazareth by accurately identifying a similarity and/or difference between the significance of the writings of two of the above as historical sources for the existence of Jesus of Nazareth. Possible points: JOSEPHUS - Jewish historian who accepted both the historical reality of Jesus and the impact Jesus had on the people he met; similar to St Paul in that he also drew on the oral tradition from those who had personally known Jesus. TACITUS - Roman historian who said Christians got their name from Christ, who was executed by the procurator Pontius Pilate; similar to Pliny the Younger, a Roman imperial legate, who writes about Jesus as a man crucified for causing a disturbance in the Roman Empire. Other valid answers accepted. Graded: Excellent 40-34, Very Good 33-28, Good 27-22, Fair 21-16, Weak 15-10, then 9-4 and 3-0.

prompt:
Outline the particular understanding of Jesus that is emphasised for Christians today by two writers of books about Christology.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Christology is the ongoing effort to understand Jesus and the meaning of his life, death and resurrection. It answers Jesus' question, 'But who do you say that I am?' (Mark 8:29).

Elizabeth A. Johnson - 'Consider Jesus: Waves of Renewal in Christology'. Johnson is an American theologian. She sees Christian tradition as a living tradition and uses the image of waves to show how understanding of Jesus has grown. The first wave was biblical Christology: Paul's crucified and risen Christ, Mark's suffering Messiah, Matthew's new Moses, Luke's Saviour of all filled with the Holy Spirit, and John's Word made flesh. So from the very start there was more than one way of seeing Jesus. Later waves include the Councils of Nicaea (325) and Chalcedon (451), which taught that Jesus is truly God and truly human. They also include medieval and post-Tridentine Christology. In 1951 Karl Rahner urged people to look anew at Jesus, and Vatican II opened dialogue with the modern world. Johnson's point for Christians today is that each age must look at Jesus again in the light of its own experience. She also stresses what Jesus shows about equality: he did not go along with the patriarchy of his time and treated women as equals.

Dermot Lane - 'The Reality of Jesus'. Lane says renewal in theology today is 'a return to the origins of Christianity'. He speaks of the 'Christ-event': Jesus' life, death and resurrection plus what they mean for believers. He stresses balance. If we ignore Jesus' humanity, we miss how he became one of us. If we ignore his divinity, we lose faith in Christ. 'Jesus' and 'Christ' must go together. His approach is a 'low-ascending Christology'. It starts with the historical Jesus of Nazareth and then moves up to how he came to be known as Lord and Christ. This helps Christians today relate to a real, human Jesus who is also the Son of God.
marking_scheme: 40 marks, marked as 20 marks x 2 (one for each writer). Marking criteria: an excellent answer will show knowledge of trends in Christianity today by setting out accurate information on the particular understanding of Jesus that is highlighted for Christians today by two writers of books about the nature and person of Christ. Possible points: Elizabeth Johnson - emphasises gender equality in 'Waves of Renewal in Christology', presenting the idea that Christians can learn from Jesus in that he did not conform to the patriarchy of his time; Jesus treated women as equals. Jurgen Moltmann - in 'The Way of Jesus Christ' emphasises Jesus' total empathy with the suffering of humanity; hope in the Resurrection offers possibilities for change in this world; an eschatological future beyond human imagining. Note: if accurate information is given without reference to two writers of books about Christology, the examiner consults the Advising Examiner. Marked as 20 marks x 2 (one 20-mark grade for each of the two parts). Each graded: Excellent 20-17, Very Good 16-14, Good 13-11, Fair 10-8, Weak 7-5, then 4-2 and 1-0.

prompt:
Profile the origins and implications of the relationship between Christianity and Judaism using one of the following headings:
- A CELEBRATING TRADITION
- THE COMMUNITY OF BELIEVERS
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Heading: A Celebrating Tradition.

Origins: Christianity grew out of Judaism. The greatest gift of Judaism to Christianity is Jesus himself, who was a Jew. To understand Jesus, Christians must appreciate his Jewishness. Most of the first Christians were Jewish, and their worship, prayer and way of organising became the foundation of Church practice. Jesus kept the Jewish festivals. He travelled to Jerusalem for Passover like other devout Jews, and on the night before he died he celebrated Passover with his disciples.

Passover (Pesach) is an eight-day festival that celebrates God freeing the Jewish people from slavery in Egypt. At the Seder meal at home the Haggadah, the story of the Exodus, is read. Children take part by asking, 'Why is this night different from all other nights?', and matzah (unleavened bread) is eaten. It is a memorial: the past is remembered so that each generation knows it was set free by God.

At that Passover meal, the Last Supper, Jesus took bread and the cup and said, 'This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me' (Luke 22:19). He offered himself in a new covenant. So the Christian Eucharist is rooted in the Jewish Passover. Both are memorial celebrations, and both use bread and wine as symbols.

Other shared roots: Christians and Jews share the Hebrew Bible (Old Testament). Both treasure the Psalms and the prophets. Christian fixed times of daily prayer have Jewish roots, and Hebrew words like Amen, Alleluia and Messiah are used in Christian worship.

Implications: Because their celebrations share the same roots, Christians cannot fully understand their own worship without Judaism. This calls for respect and dialogue. Sadly, centuries of anti-Semitism, often started or ignored by the Church, caused deep hurt. Today the Church has tried to heal this. Pope John Paul II called Jews 'our beloved elder brothers' and asked forgiveness at Yad Vashem in 2000. Groups like the Council of Christians and Jews and the Sisters of Sion work for reconciliation.
marking_scheme: 40 marks, graded. Marking criteria: an excellent answer will show knowledge of Christianity and Judaism by accurately tracing the connection between Christianity and Judaism as either a celebrating tradition or a community of believers. Possible points: A CELEBRATING TRADITION e.g. Christianity and Judaism share some symbols and rituals, e.g. the Christian Eucharist is rooted in the Jewish Passover as Jesus and his disciples were Jewish; both are memorial celebrations with symbols such as bread and wine. THE COMMUNITY OF BELIEVERS e.g. in both, the community gathers on a set day of the week (Sabbath day) to worship; this tradition derives from the Decalogue/Ten Commandments. Graded: Excellent 40-34, Very Good 33-28, Good 27-22, Fair 21-16, Weak 15-10, then 9-4 and 3-0.

prompt:
BUDDHISM / CHRISTIANITY / HINDUISM / ISLAM / JUDAISM
Examine the main forms and purpose of inter-faith dialogue between two of the world religions listed above.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Inter-faith dialogue is dialogue between different faiths, here Christianity and Judaism. It is different from ecumenism, which is dialogue between Christian churches.

Forms of dialogue:
1. Official Church teaching and gestures. Vatican II's Nostra Aetate says, 'The Catholic Church rejects nothing in those religions which is true and holy.' In 1986 Pope John Paul II visited the synagogue in Rome and called Jews 'our beloved elder brothers'. At Yad Vashem, the Holocaust memorial, in 2000 he asked forgiveness and said, 'We wish to remember... to ensure that never again will evil prevail.'
2. Organisations. The Council of Christians and Jews fosters dialogue through education, dialogue and social action. The Sisters of Sion are a religious order working for Jewish-Christian reconciliation.
3. Shared prayer and worship. In 1986 Pope John Paul II prayed at Assisi with Jews, Muslims, Hindus and Buddhists. Inter-faith worship and inter-faith prayer rooms in airports and shopping centres also bring people together.
4. Conferences. Theologians and scholars meet to explore questions like suffering, evil and the mystery of life in a non-threatening, non-competitive setting.

Purpose of dialogue:
- To heal historic wounds. Centuries of anti-Semitism, often started or ignored by the Church, left deep hurt. The German Bishops (1980) said anti-Semitism is ultimately against Christ himself.
- To build mutual respect, co-operation and reconciliation in today's multi-faith societies.
- To find common ground. Christians and Jews share the Hebrew Bible, belief in one creator God, and the dignity of people made in God's image.
- To serve humanity together. S.A. Nigosian calls this the 'dialogic' approach: finding 'a common ground to serve humanity in co-operation with one another'.
- To help each faith grow. Paul Knitter says religions must 'speak and listen to each other' and 'grow with and from each other'.

True dialogue is honest: as the World Council of Churches says, partners come 'not as manipulators but as genuine fellow-pilgrims'.
marking_scheme: 40 marks, graded. Marking criteria: an excellent answer will show knowledge of inter-faith dialogue by looking closely at the main forms and aim of inter-faith dialogue between two of the world religions listed in the question. Possible points: inter-faith dialogue can take place between individuals and communities, e.g. a prayer service; the aim can be to increase mutual understanding and respect for other religious traditions and to nourish good relationships. e.g. the Council of Christians and Jews - CCJ works in areas of education, dialogue and social action. e.g. the Assisi Day for Peace - religious leaders from all over the world gather for a day of prayer. Note: allow descriptive answers. Graded: Excellent 40-34, Very Good 33-28, Good 27-22, Fair 21-16, Weak 15-10, then 9-4 and 3-0.

prompt:
THE HEBREWS / THE GREEKS / THE ROMANS
Outline how a moral issue caused concern for the members of two of the above ancient civilisations.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The Hebrews: freedom and justice. For the Hebrews, morality was part of their relationship with God. Human responsibility came from the reality of God, and the Torah shaped how they lived. A key moral concern was freedom. Since the Exodus, when God freed them from slavery in Egypt, the Hebrews valued freedom so that they could serve God. Later persecution made this value even stronger. Closely linked was justice. The prophets and psalms condemned personal and social injustice as sinful (Amos, Micah, Psalms 9 and 10). God was seen as caring for the powerless - the widow, the orphan and the stranger - so the community had a duty to care for the poor. The Talmud asks why a workman should risk his life on high scaffolding 'if you do not pay him his wages as soon as they are due?' Inhumanity was an insult to a God of justice.

The Romans: war. The Romans were strongly influenced by the Stoics, who taught that one universal spirit lives in all people, so all should live in mutual love and rank and wealth do not matter. A major moral concern for them was when war could be justified. The orator Marcus Tullius Cicero (106-43 BCE), a Stoic, wrote about this in De Officiis. He taught that the only good reason for war is so that we might live unharmed in peace. No war should start without an official demand for satisfaction, or a formal declaration after a proper warning. War could be fought to keep a city safe, protect the innocent, avenge wrongs and honour pledges to allies. After victory, mercy should be shown to the defeated. A war without a just cause was wrong. Cicero's ideas later influenced St Augustine and the Church's teaching on war.

Possible points: THE HEBREWS e.g. freedom to devote their lives to the service of God, e.g. the Exodus experience. THE GREEKS e.g. Socrates, who was concerned with what makes a good life. THE ROMANS e.g. war - Cicero in 'De Officiis' stated that wars undertaken without cause are unjust. Note: allow descriptive answers. prompt:
Profile how a balance between personal and community values is expressed in two different charters that you have studied.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
A personal value is a quality an individual sees as good and important, such as health or freedom. A community value seeks the good of the whole community. Sometimes these clash, so a balance is needed. Two charters that express community values are the Ten Commandments and the United Nations Declaration of Human Rights.

The Ten Commandments (the Decalogue). These are recorded twice in the Bible, in Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5. They are part of the Covenant God made with his people after freeing them from Egypt. The first three commandments - have no other gods, do not take God's name in vain, keep the Sabbath holy - are about each believer's personal relationship with God. The other seven - honour your parents, do not kill, do not commit adultery, do not steal, do not bear false witness, do not covet - protect the life, family, property and good name of others. So they stress community values. The commandments are followed as one unit: they join love of God and love of neighbour, so religious life and social life are one. In this way personal faith and the good of the community are held in balance.

The UN Declaration of Human Rights. After the Second World War the United Nations agreed this charter. Its preamble calls it 'a common standard of achievement for all peoples and all nations'. It grew out of Enlightenment ideas of liberty and equality. It protects the rights of each individual, such as freedom and dignity. But every personal right carries a responsibility to respect the same right in others. For example, my freedom to live as I wish is limited by others' right to safety and peace. This creates a balance between personal and community values, so that each person's dignity is protected within a fair society for all.

Possible points: e.g. the Ten Commandments - the first three commandments refer to personal values to do with the believer's relationship with God; the remaining seven stress the importance of community values. e.g. the UN Declaration of Human Rights - every personal right within the charter carries with it a responsibility; this creates a balance between personal and community values. prompt:
'The unexamined life is not worth living.'
Imagine Socrates was alive today and giving a talk on this topic.
Based on your knowledge of Socrates' thinking, outline two points that he would make about the purpose of life for people today.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Point 1: Know how little you know. Socrates would tell people today that the purpose of life begins with honest questioning. At his trial he said his only wisdom was knowing how little he knew. Most people think they know more than they do. He spent his life asking 'innocent' questions of so-called experts to show the gaps in their thinking. Today we can find instant answers online, but the questions that really matter need deep thought. Socrates would say: do not just accept what social media, advertising or popular opinion tells you. Stop and examine your own beliefs. That is what 'the unexamined life is not worth living' means. Great thinkers since, such as Rene Descartes with his 'method of doubt', followed this lead.

Point 2: Care for your soul and live a life of virtue. Socrates said the Athenians cared for wealth, status and their bodies but neglected the soul. He would say the same about a society that measures success by money, looks and followers. For Socrates, wealth, beauty or strength cannot create virtue, but virtue creates everything that is truly good. He said, 'The really important thing is not to live but to live well.' He also taught that all virtue is knowledge: if you truly know what is right, you will do it, and wrongdoing comes from ignorance. Pleasure is good, but lasting happiness only comes from a virtuous life. Against the Sophists, who said whatever suits the strongest is right, he would remind people that what pleases us is not always good, and that we must act for the common good. So the purpose of life for people today is to seek wisdom, act justly and be good, not just to be comfortable or successful.
marking_scheme: 20 marks x 2 (two points, 20 marks each). prompt:
Explain how two aspects of living in society today could block people from searching for the meaning of life.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Aspect 1: Consumerism and materialism. Society today tells us that happiness can be found in material things. We are bombarded with advertising promising that we will be happy if we buy a product, drive a certain car or wear certain clothes. This blocks the search for meaning because it fills our minds with the next purchase instead of the big questions such as 'Why am I here?' Human experience shows that things do not bring lasting happiness. This is called hedonic adaptation: people return to a set level of happiness. Elizabeth Scott's study found that lotto winners went back to roughly their old level of happiness after about a year, and some became less happy. A new phone gives a short burst of joy, and soon we want a newer one. Buddhism teaches that suffering comes from desire and attachment (tanha). While people chase things, they avoid the deeper questions.

Aspect 2: Busyness and exhaustion. Our fast-paced world values speed, efficiency and productivity. Many people are simply too busy or too tired to stop and ask what life is for. Being 'too busy' can become an excuse to avoid the big questions. In Robin Sharma's book The Monk Who Sold His Ferrari, Julian Mantle is a rich lawyer with a mansion and a Ferrari, but he is stressed and unhappy. Only after a heart attack in a courtroom does he stop, sell everything and go in search of meaning in the Himalayas. The sages teach him to respect his time, serve others and live in the present moment. The message is that most people waste the time they have, and only when we become aware of how we spend our time can we find meaning. Abraham Maslow also showed that people must meet basic needs first, so stress about work and money can leave no room for reflection.

prompt:
Describe one example of how the philosophical thinking in Ancient Greece can be seen as a key moment in the development of philosophy.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
One key moment was the work of Socrates in fifth-century BCE Athens, which turned philosophy towards the human person, honest questioning and the search for virtue.

Before this, pre-Socratic thinkers such as Thales and Heraclitus mostly asked about the natural world: how the universe began and what it is made of. In democratic Athens the Sophists shifted the focus to the human person and their place in the world. But the Sophists taught rhetoric to win arguments, charged high fees and taught that truth is relative. Protagoras said, 'Man is the measure of all things,' and Thrasymachus said that justice is 'the interest of the stronger'.

Socrates challenged this. He was a ceaseless questioner who used questions to expose gaps in people's reasoning and get closer to the truth. He said his only wisdom was knowing how little he knew (Socratic ignorance). This showed that a thinker must question his own assumptions before forming a theory. Later, Rene Descartes built on this with his 'method of doubt'. Socrates also wanted a universal definition of justice, against the Sophists' relativism. He taught that we must care for the soul above all, that virtue is knowledge and that virtue is necessary for happiness. He was the first to think seriously about virtue.

His influence was huge. His pupil Plato wrote dialogues in which ideas are tested through debate, and founded the Academy, the forerunner of the modern university. Plato taught Aristotle, the 'father of Western logic'. Aristotle and the Roman Stoics started their thinking on virtue from Socrates, and Alasdair MacIntyre's book After Virtue shows it is still a major concern today. Socrates was sentenced to death in 399 BCE, but his belief that 'the unexamined life is not worth living' became a foundation stone of Western philosophy. This is why Ancient Greece is seen as a key moment in the development of philosophy.

prompt:
Imagine that Anselm and Aquinas are taking part in a discussion about the existence of God with people today.
Outline the ideas that each could put forward to prove the existence of God for people today.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
St Anselm (1033-1109): Anselm was Archbishop of Canterbury and is called the 'father of scholasticism'. He started from belief in God and used reason to show that belief makes sense. He would tell people today that God is 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived' - the greatest being we can think of. His argument has three steps: (1) 'God' means the greatest conceivable being; (2) existing in reality is greater than existing only in the mind; (3) so God must exist in reality, because if God existed only in our minds, we could think of something greater - a God who really exists. Since Kant, this is called the ontological argument. It may seem strange today, but it has a definite logic. Anselm would remind people that this 'proof' is not scientific evidence, but a signpost showing it is reasonable to believe.

St Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274): Aquinas lived when reason was admired and wanted faith to be a reasonable subject for discussion. He would start from the world we see around us and offer five proofs. (1) Prime mover: nothing moves itself, so there must be a first mover - God. (2) First cause: nothing creates itself, so there must be an uncreated creator. (3) Necessary being: everything depends on something else, so there must be a being on which all others depend. (4) Degrees of perfection: we see more and less goodness and beauty, so there must be a perfect standard - God. (5) Supreme intelligence: the universe is ordered towards regular ends, so it must be directed by an intelligent mind. Aquinas would say to people today that science can explain how things work, but it cannot explain why anything exists at all. His proofs show that faith and reason can work together.

1. The Kingdom is inclusive. Everyone is welcome at God's table. Jesus ate with tax collectors and sinners (Matthew 9:10-13) and with Simon the leper, showing that outcasts are included.

4. The Kingdom is both here now and still to come, so people must respond urgently. Jesus proclaimed, 'The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news' (Mark 1:15). He called for metanoia (a change of heart) and told people to be ready, like the ten bridesmaids (Matthew 25:1-13).

prompt:
ESSENES / SADDUCEES / ZEALOTS
Compare the reaction of two religious groups listed above to Roman rule in Palestine at the time of Jesus of Nazareth.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
The Sadducees and the Zealots reacted to Roman rule in opposite ways.

The Sadducees chose co-operation. They were mainly wealthy, powerful conservatives linked to the Temple. They had held power before the Romans came and kept it by co-operating with the 'enemy'. They were part of the puppet government that ran the law and collected taxes, and were the most powerful group in the Sanhedrin. They followed the path of least resistance.

The Zealots chose violent resistance. They were a radical, militant group who believed it was their duty to oppose the Roman presence and fight anything that threatened the Jewish faith. They looked back to the Maccabean revolt of 164 BCE. They may have appealed to those who suffered most under Rome, especially from taxes. There was no place for them in the Sanhedrin.

So the key difference is that the Sadducees worked with Rome to protect their power, while the Zealots fought Rome to free God's people. One similarity is that both reactions carried risk: the Zealots risked a violent end, and the Sadducees risked losing their Jewish identity. Neither group survived into modern times.

prompt:
Explain how returning to the original teaching of Jesus was central to the establishment of two of the following movements:
CÉILÍ DÉ / EVANGELICAL MOVEMENT OF EARLY 19TH CENTURY PROTESTANTISM / LIBERATION THEOLOGY / MENDICANT ORDERS / LUTHER'S REFORMS / SECOND VATICAN COUNCIL
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The Mendicant Orders (13th century): The Mendicant or 'begging' orders grew out of disillusionment with the Church. As towns grew, people saw the clergy as a powerful, wealthy group whose lifestyle did not match gospel values. The Mendicants returned to the poverty and simple lifestyle of Jesus in the Gospels. Members held no possessions and had the right to beg, and pastoral care was the focus of their training. St Francis of Assisi, son of a wealthy merchant, gave up his wealth at twenty for a life of poverty and preaching, and his followers wanted to imitate Christ in all things. St Dominic founded the Order of Preachers, committed to absolute poverty and preaching the gospel. Unlike other critics, they stayed within the Church, so their return to Jesus' way of life renewed it from inside.

Liberation Theology (1968 onwards): Vatican II called the Church to read the signs of the times in the light of the gospel and work against injustice. In 1968 the Latin American bishops met at Medellin in Colombia and concluded that their society was unjust, with most people living in poverty and oppression. They went back to the gospel and saw Jesus as the great liberator and his message as one of freedom for the oppressed. The Church would take the side of the poor: the preferential option for the poor. In 1971 Gustavo Gutierrez wrote A Theology of Liberation, showing its roots in the gospel. Supporters believe that working for justice is truly following Jesus. It upset people in power, and Archbishop Oscar Romero was murdered in 1980. Critics said it was too political, but supporters say it is firmly rooted in the example of Jesus Christ.

Outline the understanding of salvation/liberation found in the teaching of one of the following world religions:

Christianity is a religion of salvation and redemption. Christians believe that sin - the human failure to do God's will and live by love - separates people from God. As John 3:16 says: 'For God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.'

Christians believe Christ will judge the world at the end of time, and that the saved will share eternal happiness in heaven. This hope is celebrated at Easter, the feast of triumph over sin and death.

prompt:
Compare the understanding of salvation/liberation found in either Christianity or Judaism with that found in one of the following world religions:
BUDDHISM / HINDUISM / ISLAM
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Comparing Christianity and Buddhism.

Similarity: Both religions see salvation as freedom from what makes human life go wrong, and both say it is reached by changing how we live. For Christians the problem is sin; for Buddhists it is suffering (dukkha) caused by desire and attachment (tanha). Both call for a moral life: Christians follow Jesus' command to love, and Buddhists follow the Noble Eightfold Path of wisdom, morality and meditation.

Differences: First, who saves. Christianity is a religion of redemption: God takes the initiative and saves people through Jesus. Buddhism is a religion of self-redemption: the Buddha is not a god or a redeemer, and each person is solely responsible for their own progress to enlightenment, without the grace of a Divine Redeemer.

Second, the goal. For Christians the goal is eternal life with God in heaven after the resurrection. For Buddhists the goal is nirvana: freedom from craving and from the cycle of rebirth. Buddhists believe there is no permanent soul (anatman); rebirth happens without a soul passing from life to life. Christians believe each person lives once and hopes to rise with Christ.

prompt:
Outline how the relationship between the sacred and profane is expressed in the way two objects are used in worship by members of a major world religion.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The sacred is 'that which is set aside for religious use', while the profane is the ordinary world of everyday life. In worship, ordinary objects are often set aside so that they point to God. As Philip Barnes says, 'the sacred can take many forms' - sacred things, ceremonies and places. Two examples come from Christianity.

Object 1: Water in Baptism. Water is one of the most ordinary things in daily life - we drink it and wash with it. In Baptism, the ceremony that joins a person to the Church, water becomes the main sacred symbol. Its everyday meanings of life and cleansing are lifted up to stand for something holy: the washing away of sin, dying to the old way of life, new life in Christ and receiving the Holy Spirit. A sacrament is a symbolic word, gesture or object that makes a hidden reality visible. So the profane (ordinary water) becomes a channel for the sacred (God's grace), while still being water. This shows that the two are not completely separate: the holy is met through the ordinary.

Object 2: Bread and wine in the Eucharist. Bread and wine are everyday food and drink shared at ordinary meals. In the Eucharist they are set aside for worship and used in the liturgy, whose symbolic action is both a meal and a sacrifice. They recall the Last Supper, when Jesus asked his followers to remember him in the breaking of bread. For Christians they express the presence of Christ, the unity of believers with each other, and the sacrificial death of Christ. An ordinary family meal becomes a sacred meal of the whole community. Again, the ordinary is not rejected but made holy.

In both cases, as Mircea Eliade argued, an object becomes sacred because it points to a sacred reality beyond this world, and the worshipper is carried out of the ordinary into an experience of awe, as Rudolf Otto described.

prompt:
Outline the approach to deciding what is right and wrong that is put forward in two of the following moral philosophies/theories:
DEONTOLOGICAL ETHICS / HEDONISM / RIGHT RELATIONSHIP / TELEOLOGICAL ETHICS / UTILITARIANISM / VIRTUE ETHICS
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Deontological ethics: The word comes from the Greek deon, meaning duty or obligation. Deontological ethics says there is an objective moral law - a code of behaviour - that does not change over time or with the situation, and it tells us how we should act. Morality is seen mainly in terms of duty, law and obligation. An act is judged not by its consequences but by whether it is right or wrong according to the law, which is true in all circumstances. The deontologist asks: 'What is the law? What is my duty?' For example, a deontologist would not break a red light even in the middle of the night with no one around, and says 'I pay my taxes because that is my duty and the law demands it.' For a Christian, the moral law is inspired by the Word of God, so it is their duty to follow the Ten Commandments and the moral teaching of Jesus.

Teleological ethics: The word comes from the Greek telos, meaning end or goal. Teleological ethics judges an action by the end it achieves. Good actions lead towards our fulfilment and ultimate happiness, so the key to what is right is what will happen as a result of my action. The person asks: 'What good will this achieve?' For example, 'I pay my taxes because I want a fair opportunity in life for all,' or 'I do not smoke because it will damage my health and slow me down in sport.' Unlike deontology, the same kind of act might be judged differently if it leads to a different result. For a Christian, the ultimate goal of life is to be with God: an act is good if it leads towards that goal and evil if it stops a person reaching it.

prompt:
Explain how a moral philosophy/theory, listed below, could influence a person's decision about what is the right thing to do on an issue concerning one of the following:
CRIME & PUNISHMENT / POLITICS & ECONOMICS / MEDICAL ETHICS / RELATIONSHIPS & SEXUALITY
(Theories listed in part D (a): Deontological ethics, Hedonism, Right relationship, Teleological ethics, Utilitarianism, Virtue ethics.)
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Theory: deontological ethics. Issue (medical ethics): voluntary euthanasia.

Imagine a person whose elderly parent is terminally ill and in great pain, and who asks for help to end their life. This is a medical ethics issue. Seeing a loved one suffer is terrible, and some people come to support active euthanasia because of the suffering and the idea of 'death with dignity'.

A deontologist would approach this decision by asking: 'What is the law? What is my duty?' Deontological ethics says there is an objective moral law that does not change with the situation, and acts are judged by that law, not by their consequences. So even if ending the parent's life would end their pain, the deontologist cannot decide simply on the basis of the good outcome. The end does not justify the means.

The moral law forbids taking another person's life. This would influence the person to decide that euthanasia is wrong. It goes against the civil law in most countries, against the moral law and against natural law. For a religious person, taking life is taking God's place, since God is the giver of life. Pope John Paul II's Evangelium vitae argues from this duty to God's law. If the person were a doctor, the duty of care would be primary: the doctor's role is to heal and care, not to kill.

However, the deontologist also has a duty to care for the suffering parent. So they would not walk away. They would distinguish between killing and relieving pain. They could choose good palliative care, such as the hospice movement, which has made great advances in pain management. The Church of England's On Dying Well makes this point: a sick person is of no less value because they cannot contribute, and love extends especially to the helpless.

So deontological ethics would lead the person to refuse active euthanasia, because their duty to the moral law of respect for life comes first, while still fulfilling their duty of love by making sure the parent is cared for and kept as comfortable as possible.

prompt:
Imagine the Sophists of Ancient Greece were advertising courses in philosophy.
Based on your knowledge of the Sophists outline what you think they would say about philosophy and the purpose it serves in the lives of people.

model_answer:
COURSES IN PHILOSOPHY - TAUGHT BY THE SOPHISTS OF ATHENS

Do you want to succeed in public life? Athens is a democracy. Free citizens run the state, and judges and officials are chosen by lot. To get on in politics or the law courts, you must be well educated. We, the Sophists, can train you - for a fee.

Who are we? The word 'Sophist' roughly means 'professor'. We come from different parts of Greece. We are wise and well travelled, and we teach in all the major cities.

What will you learn? Poetry, grammar, mythology, religion, literature, statesmanship and generalship. But our key skill is rhetoric - the use of language to influence or persuade. We will teach you to argue both sides of a case equally fiercely, whether you agree or not. You will learn how to win debates and win lawsuits.

What is philosophy for? For us, philosophy is not a search for some fixed truth. It is about the human person and their place in the world. Our great teacher Protagoras says, 'Man is the measure of all things.' Truth is relative: if one person says it is hot and another says it is not, both are true for them. Gorgias says there is no way to tell knowledge from opinion, because we filter everything through our own thoughts and words. So morality is up to the individual. Thrasymachus even says 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger.'

So the purpose of philosophy in your life is practical: it gives you the power to persuade, to succeed and to get ahead. Unlike the old thinkers such as Thales, who asked what the universe is made of, we put people at the centre of thought. We also show that every idea must be debated and challenged.

(Critics like Socrates and Plato say we care more about money than truth, and that our relativism leads to moral breakdown. But our students admire our questioning attitude.)

prompt:
Since ancient times people have used rites to mark key moments in life -
- RITE OF BURIAL
- RITE OF INITIATION & PASSAGE
Explain how evidence of religious belief can be seen in each of the above rites associated with people who lived in ancient times.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Rite of burial
Burial rituals show how ancient people viewed life, death and the afterlife. Formal burial was an important step: bodies were no longer abandoned or left to wild animals. People moved beyond seeing death as the end and looked for ways for life to continue. In Moravia, a mass grave 25,000-30,000 years old held eighteen people - ten children and eight adults - buried with ornaments and objects in an oval pit covered with stone slabs and mammoth bones. Such care shows something significant was intended. At Catalhoyuk in Turkey (about 6250-5400 BCE), families buried their dead under the floors of their houses, which may show a belief that the dead were still part of the living. At Newgrange (about 3200 BCE) the mound was used for burial and for winter solstice rituals. Other burial symbols also point to belief: seeds in a tomb may suggest belief in rebirth, red ochre may suggest the life-giving power of blood, and rich ornaments may show belief in an afterlife. These symbols are evidence of a spiritual or religious dimension to life.

Rite of initiation and passage
Rites of passage mark important changes in life, such as moving from childhood to adulthood. They follow three stages, named by Arnold van Gennep: separation, transition and incorporation. They show an early human need to be in harmony with the cosmos, so they can be seen as early religious belief. Among the Murngin of Australia, a boy is told the 'Great Father Snake' is calling him. A horn called Yurlunggur is blown - the call of the snake. Over many nights he is shown dances of his ancestors and taught sacred myths, then sent on a journey before circumcision. Among the Arunta, bullroarers sound to symbolise the voices of the deities. Joseph Campbell says the boys are symbolically killed and reborn as adults. The belief in spirit beings and sacred myths shows clear religious belief.

prompt:
Experiences in life can be understood in different ways -
- THE AESTHETIC
- THE PROPHETIC
Using examples, explain how a relationship with God/gods/the divine can be expressed in each of the above ways of interpreting human experience.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The aesthetic
The aesthetic interpretation is an artistic understanding of life. Creative people express their relationship with God through music, painting, sculpture and poetry. Great beauty suggests God's presence, and art has expressed belief in God since earliest times. For example, Marc Chagall, probably the most prominent Jewish painter of the twentieth century, painted White Crucifixion. Jesus the Jew is shown crucified, wearing a prayer shawl, between communist soldiers and Nazis attacking a synagogue. For Chagall, Jesus on the cross stood for the suffering of all Jewish people in an apparently God-forsaken world. It is a favourite of Pope Francis. Another example is the singer Lauren Daigle, whose song 'You Say' expresses who we are in God's eyes, even when the world says otherwise. In both, beauty becomes a way of meeting God.

The prophetic
A prophet examines and criticises society in the light of religious belief. Rooted in prayer, the prophet seeks to know God's will and speaks out for justice, because injustice that causes suffering offends God. Its roots lie in Amos, Jeremiah, Isaiah, John the Baptist and Jesus. Fr Peter McVerry SJ is a modern example. Since 1974 he has worked with homeless and disadvantaged young people in Dublin. He questions a society that tolerates inequality and calls for a truly Christian response to poverty. His Peter McVerry Trust works to reduce homelessness. He says those in the shadows are 'God's favourites'. Here a relationship with God is shown by speaking out on God's behalf for the poor.

prompt:
- ATHEISM
- REDUCTIONISM
Compare the approach that would be taken by each of the above points of view to answering a question about the meaning of life.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Atheism is the denial of the existence of God. Reductionism means reducing something to its smallest parts. Both are non-religious responses to life's big questions, but they approach the meaning of life in different ways.

Atheism's approach: An atheist answers the question 'What is the meaning of life?' without any reference to God. There is no divine plan and no afterlife, so meaning must be found in this life. Theoretical atheists may reject God because they see science and religion as incompatible, or because evil and suffering make a loving God impossible. Practical atheists simply see the question of God as irrelevant. Militant atheists argue religious belief is harmful and holds back human potential. So for the atheist, people create their own meaning, for example through relationships, work or helping others.

Reductionism's approach: Reductionism began as a scientific method - for example, moving from earth, air, fire and water to subatomic theory. As a worldview it says humans are part of the physical world and nothing more. If something cannot be studied scientifically, it cannot be known. It rules out opinion, feeling and belief. A reductionist would break the question down into physical facts: a human is atoms and DNA.

Similarities: Both leave out God and the spiritual. Both rely on reason and the natural world.

Differences: Atheism is mainly about denying God, but an atheist can still value love, justice and happiness as real sources of meaning. Reductionism goes further: it denies we are more than the sum of our parts. Just as a novel is more than letters, critics say a person is more than atoms. So reductionism risks losing higher meaning altogether, while atheism still looks for meaning within human life.

Implicit reference to similarities and/or differences is allowed. topic_label: Jesus as a threat to Rome
prompt:
Explain two reasons why the teaching of Jesus of Nazareth would have posed a threat for the Roman rulers in Palestine.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Reason 1: The Kingdom of God. Jesus proclaimed the Kingdom of God. The Romans could have seen this as a direct challenge to the rule of Caesar and the power of Imperial Rome. At his trial Pilate asked, 'Are you the King of the Jews?' (John 18:33). Jesus said his kingdom was 'not from this world', but he did not deny being a king. This gave the Romans an excuse to charge him with treason. His enemies also accused him of 'forbidding us to pay taxes to the emperor, and saying that he himself is the Messiah, a king' (Luke 23:2).

Reason 2: A new set of values. Jesus was not a military threat, but his message challenged the values of the empire. In God's kingdom the first would be last and the last first, the poor would be blessed and those who suffered would rejoice. Care for others would be the sign of God's presence. This turned Roman ideas of power and status upside down. Jesus challenged not only those in power but the nature of power itself. For this reason he was charged with treason and crucified.

prompt:
Examine why the Jewish authorities in Palestine were challenged by the actions of Jesus of Nazareth.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
The Jewish religious leaders - the Pharisees, scribes, Sadducees and chief priests - were challenged by Jesus because his actions threatened their interpretation of the Law and their authority.

First, Jesus followed the spirit of the Law, while the Pharisees read it very literally. In Luke 14:1-6, in the home of a leading Pharisee, Jesus healed a man with dropsy on the Sabbath. He asked, 'If one of you has a child or an ox that has fallen into a well, will you not immediately pull it out on a sabbath day?' They could not answer. He showed that helping someone in need matters more than the rule against Sabbath work.

Second, Jesus forgave sins. When a paralysed man was let down through a roof, Jesus said, 'Son, your sins are forgiven.' The scribes believed only God could forgive sin, so to them this was blasphemy.

Third, at Passover Jesus cleansed the Temple (Mark 11:15-18). He overturned the tables of the money-changers and said they had made God's house 'a den of robbers'. This directly challenged the Temple and the authority of the Sadducees and Pharisees. The chief priests and scribes then looked for a way to kill him, because the crowd was spellbound by his teaching.
marking_scheme: An excellent answer will show an understanding of the religious context in Palestine at the time of Jesus of Nazareth by looking closely at one or more accurate reasons why the Jewish authorities were challenged by the words or deeds of Jesus of Nazareth. prompt:
Compare the understanding of Jesus that is emphasised by a writer of books about Christology with the way Jesus is portrayed in the Gospels.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Christology is the continuing effort to understand Jesus and the meaning of his life, death and resurrection. It tries to answer Jesus' question in Mark 8:29: 'But who do you say that I am?'

Jesus in the Gospels: From the beginning there was more than one portrait of Jesus. Elizabeth Johnson calls this biblical Christology. Mark shows Jesus as the suffering Messiah. Matthew shows him as the new Moses, the teacher of the new Law. Luke shows him filled with the Holy Spirit, the Saviour of all. John shows him as the Word of God made flesh. The Gospels tell the story of what Jesus did and said - his teaching, miracles, death and resurrection - and they are written from faith.

Dermot Lane, 'The Reality of Jesus': Lane says renewal in theology is 'a return to the origins of Christianity'. He speaks of the 'Christ-event': the life, death and resurrection of Jesus plus what they mean for believers. He insists on balance: if we ignore Jesus' humanity we miss how he became one of us; if we ignore his divinity we miss faith in Christ. 'Jesus' (the historical man) and 'Christ' (the chosen one, Son of God) go together. His approach is a low-ascending Christology: start with the historical Jesus, then move to how he became known as Lord and Christ.

Similarities: Both centre on the life, death and resurrection of Jesus. Both hold that the Jesus of history is the Christ of faith, and both aim to help people know and follow him.

Differences: The Gospels are stories written for early communities, each stressing one image of Jesus. Lane is a modern theologian who reflects on the Gospels in a systematic way. The early Church began with faith in the risen Christ, whereas Lane, like many since the nineteenth century, begins with the historical Jesus 'from below' and works upwards. He also brings later teaching, such as Chalcedon's 'truly God and truly human', into dialogue with the Gospel picture.

Implicit reference to a writer of books about Christology is allowed. prompt:
Describe two ideas that are particularly associated with primal religion.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Idea 1: Mana. Mana is a Melanesian idea. It is power embedded in an object or person. It comes from kinship with gods and ancestors. Some people, places or things have more mana than others - for example, tribal chiefs embody the mana of their people and land. Mana is an impersonal force: it is how the spirit world shows itself. Meetings between different kinds of mana are tense and even dangerous, so boundaries called tabu are set up.

Idea 2: Tabu (taboo). Tabu is a Polynesian idea. A tabu person, object or place is 'set apart', removed from everyday use and consecrated for ritual and worship. Rules of tabu protect the power of mana. Sacred objects such as vessels, dance masks and head-dresses can only be used by mana-filled people who are ritually pure. Rules of washing, purification, touch and sound keep their 'otherness'. Breaking these rules needs reparation or sacrifice to avoid the punishment of illness.
marking_scheme: 10 marks for each idea (10M x 2). prompt:
Explain how the influence of two ideas associated with primal religion can be seen in a major world religion that you have studied.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
World religion: Islam.

Idea 1: Tabu - the sacred set apart. In primal religion, tabu places and objects are set apart for worship, and rules of washing and purification protect their holiness. This influence can be seen in Islam. The Ka'ba in Mecca is the most sacred shrine, set apart as the goal of the Hajj pilgrimage. Its black cloth is renewed every year, and the old cloth is cut up and kept as relics. Before daily prayer (salat), Muslims perform ritual washing called wudu - if there is no water, clean sand can be used. Like tabu rules, this marks the move from ordinary life into the holy.

Idea 2: Offerings and sacrifice. Primal peoples made offerings and sacrifices to honour, praise or thank the spirits and gods. This idea lives on in Islam in the festival of Eid-ul-Adha, the Festival of Sacrifices, held worldwide at the end of the Hajj. Giving is also an act of worship in zakat, the giving of alms to the poor (generally 2.5 per cent of income), which is believed to purify the soul. As in primal religion, giving something of value expresses devotion and dependence on God.

prompt:
Choose one world religion from List A and one world religion from List B below:
LIST A: Christianity, Judaism
LIST B: Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam
Compare the role being part of a community plays in the lives of believers within the world religions that you have chosen above.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
I have chosen Christianity (List A) and Islam (List B).

Christianity: For all Christian churches, community is central. Following Christ means an active community life of fellowship, prayer and service. The early Church saw itself as the Body of Christ, where every member had a role - to be a sign of God's love and to support one another in crisis. Since Vatican II the Catholic Church sees itself as the People of God, united by faith and joined by baptism. Christians join the community through Baptism, and the Eucharist celebrates Christ's presence with the community. Fr Niall O'Brien said there is 'no Christianity without community': a believing, sharing community that looks after the poor and speaks out for justice. Taizé in France shows community rising above denominational differences.

Islam: Muslims belong to the Umma, the worldwide community of Muslims. It is organised by the Qur'an and the Sharia, which cover relationships with God, with one another and with society - law, trade, politics and social justice. The Five Pillars build a sense of community regardless of race, colour, language or position. Friday noon prayer takes place together at the mosque, a centre of prayer, education and social life. Zakat, giving to the poor, is an act of worship. Worship is truly meaningful only in community, because believing in the unity of Allah (tauhid) also means unity among all creation.

Similarities: In both, community shapes daily life, worship and care for the poor. Both gather weekly to pray together, and both see helping the needy as part of faith.

Differences: Christianity is divided into many churches with different structures and an ordained clergy. In Islam the imam is a teacher and community leader, not an ordained priest. Islam also joins religion and society together through Sharia, while many Western Christians separate church and state.

prompt:
- CRIME AND PUNISHMENT
- MEDICAL ETHICS
- POLITICS AND ECONOMICS
- RELATIONSHIPS AND SEXUALITY
- VIOLENCE
Examine how Jesus' teaching on 'right relationship' would influence Christians in deciding what is right or wrong about two of the issues listed above.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Jesus' teaching on right relationship means living in right relationship with God, neighbour, self and the world. All his moral teaching is summed up in one command: love God and love your neighbour as yourself (Mark 12:28-34). This love is agape - unselfish love that seeks only the good of the other.

Issue 1: Violence
In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus said, 'Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you... If anyone strikes you on the right cheek, turn the other also.' He also said, 'Blessed are the peacemakers.' A Christian deciding about violence would ask whether it respects the dignity of every person, even an enemy. The early Christians were basically pacifist; Origen taught that 'Christians do not go forth as soldiers', because the love command seemed to rule out shedding blood. Today Quakers and Mennonites refuse military service for this reason. The Catholic Church still holds the Just War theory but has moved strongly towards pacifism. So Jesus' teaching leads Christians to see violence as a last resort at most, and to work for peace and dialogue.

Issue 2: Crime and punishment
Jesus is on the side of people: 'The Sabbath was made for humankind, not humankind for the Sabbath.' He said, 'What I want is mercy, not sacrifice,' and he was gracious and forgiving to sinners, as in the parable of the Prodigal Son. He did not encourage 'quid pro quo' justice. So a Christian would judge that punishment should protect society but also respect the dignity of the offender and leave room for repentance and conversion (metanoia). This is why many Christians oppose the death penalty. Pope John Paul II's Evangelium vitae said cases where it could be justified are 'rare, if not non-existent', because human dignity stays with a person whatever they have done.

prompt:
Individual rights need to be balanced with the common good.
Assess the evidence for this statement making reference to one example from either Irish civil law or an international charter.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The common good is what is best for the whole of society. It tries to help people cooperate so that everyone can be fulfilled, and it is a counter-balance to excessive individualism. Individual rights are the personal freedoms each person has. Sometimes what is good for the community is not good for the person, so the two must be balanced.

Irish civil law clearly tries to strike this balance. When the Constitution was debated in 1937, Eamon de Valera said the law must make sure 'the rights of the individual... and the rights of a community... do not conflict and properly coordinate.' Personal rights are protected in Articles 40-44 of the Constitution, but they are not absolute and are balanced with the common good.

Example: the Derrynaflan Hoard. In 1980 Mr Webb and his son found the Derrynaflan Hoard - an eighth-century silver chalice, strainer and stand - in County Tipperary. They were trespassing, but handed it to the National Museum expecting full compensation. The court ruled that the State's right to own national treasure, for the common good of all Irish people, was a higher value than the rights of the finders. As a gesture of goodwill they were given 25,000 pounds.

Assessment: This case is strong evidence for the statement. The finders' rights were not ignored - they received a payment - but the common good won because the hoard is part of everyone's heritage. Other cases support this: Noel and Marie Murray, prisoners serving life sentences, lost their claim to conjugal visits because society's need for protection came first. However, the evidence also shows the balance is not always fair. In the Barbato Borza case, a compulsory purchase order took his shop, and he says it was later sold to a developer for 'a profit of millions' while he received nothing. This shows the common good can be used to trample individual rights, as strict utilitarianism does. So the statement is true, but the balance must be carefully protected so that it respects the dignity of each person.
marking_scheme: An excellent answer will show an understanding of personal and communal values by accurately judging the extent to which either one Irish civil law or an international charter shows evidence that an individual's rights need to be balanced with what is regarded as best for society as a whole. prompt:
Imagine you have the chance to talk with Aristotle about the impact of his ideas on philosophy and scientific thinking.
Outline two points that you would make about the way Aristotle's ideas contributed to philosophy and scientific thinking.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Point 1: You moved philosophy from abstract forms to real things we can observe.

Your teacher Plato said that ideal forms, like 'roundness' or 'justice', exist on their own and are more real than the objects we see. You disagreed. You argued that the individual, real object is what truly exists, and forms exist only because we observe them in real things. You explained this with substantial form (a form that cannot change without the object changing its nature) and accidental form (a surface feature). For example, painting a round white stone red is only an accidental change. This meant that knowledge begins with the senses: we study the real world first and then reason about it. In Raphael's painting The School of Athens, Plato points up to the heavens but you gesture out to the world. That focus on observation is why you are called the founding father of the natural sciences, such as biology and zoology, and the 'father of Western logic'. It paved the way for thinking based on experiment and reason, and thinkers like St Thomas Aquinas built on your ideas of matter and form.

Point 2: You asked what causes things, and argued for a first cause.

Science explains our experiences by finding their causes, and you gave the first systematic analysis of causation. In your Metaphysics you argued that everything around us changes and perishes, so there must be an unchanging, imperishable 'unmoved mover' that sets everything in motion. This first cause cannot be physical, so it must be immaterial - pure thought. It moves things not by pushing them but by being their goal, the ultimate good, like a magnet drawing metal. Your picture of an ordered universe, set in motion by an intelligent being, meant the universe could be understood by reason. This made physics possible, refuted the Sophists' relativism, and deeply influenced later thinkers such as Plotinus and Aquinas.

An excellent answer shows knowledge of philosophical thought in ancient Greece by setting out accurate information on two ways that Aristotle's ideas influenced philosophical and scientific thinking. Points of reference, e.g.: Aristotle disagreed with Plato's claim that it is the universals, the forms/ideas that exist; for Aristotle it is the individual substance that really exists; he recognised that knowledge begins with the senses but then moves to a broader understanding of its purpose and potentiality as a whole; his idea of prime matter and substantial form helped to develop scientific thought as it paved the way for logical thought based on experiment and reason. Aristotle provided the first systematic analysis of the nature of causation; science is dedicated to explaining the reason for experiences by uncovering their cause(s); Aristotle recognised that the intelligibility of the universe, and so the possibility of physics, depended on acknowledging a first cause. Other valid points accepted. Marked 20 + 20 (20 marks for each of the two points). Each half is graded on four criteria: evidence of the marking criteria, relevance, use of skill, factual accuracy. prompt:
Explain how questions about the meaning of life were expressed in two myths associated with people who lived in ancient times.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Myths are symbolic stories, passed down by word of mouth, that came before philosophy and science. They are the earliest evidence of humanity's search for meaning, because they try to answer life's key questions.

Myth 1: The Epic of Gilgamesh (Mesopotamia, modern Iraq)
This myth asks: Why do we die, and is there such a thing as eternal life? Gilgamesh was a legendary king. After the death of his friend Enkidu, he set out on a dangerous journey to find the secret of eternal life. The goddess Ishtar told him to stop: 'When the gods created man, they put death upon mankind, and held life in their own hands.' She said he should enjoy the mortal joys of life instead. He kept going, and Utnapishtim told him of a plant at the bottom of the cosmic sea that makes a man young again. Gilgamesh dived down and plucked it, but on the way home a serpent ate it while he slept. Gilgamesh sat down and wept. The myth expresses the human fear of death and the belief that no one can escape the mortal human condition. It also answers a smaller question: why snakes shed their skin.

Myth 2: The Myth of Prometheus (Ancient Greece)
This myth asks: Where does human suffering come from, and what are the gods like? Zeus was angry with humanity and took away their fire. Prometheus, a mediator between gods and mortals, stole fire from the Sun and gave it to mankind. Zeus swore revenge. Prometheus was chained to a pillar while an eagle tore at his liver every day. Zeus also had Pandora made. She opened a jar holding all the Spites that plague mankind - Old Age, Labour, Sickness, Insanity, Vice and Passion - and they attacked the human race. So the myth explains suffering as a punishment from the gods. It also shows Zeus as a vengeful god to be feared, and Prometheus as a force for good.

An excellent answer shows an understanding of symbolic language by giving an accurate account of how questions about the meaning of life can be seen in two myths associated with people who lived in the very distant past. Gilgamesh sets out to discover a flower that will grant him eternal life and just as it is in his grasp it slips away, showing that it is impossible to escape the mortal human condition. The myth of Prometheus - what is the origin of human suffering? Human suffering is seen as a punishment from the gods; Prometheus steals fire from the gods and gives it to humans; the god Zeus introduces suffering into the world as a punishment. Other valid myths accepted. Marked 20 + 20 (20 marks for each of the two points). Each half is graded on four criteria: evidence of the marking criteria, relevance, use of skill, factual accuracy.
