prompt:
The development of philosophy can be traced back to Ancient Greece.
Explain why two other points in time can be described as key moments in the development of philosophical thought.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Key moment 1: The medieval Christian philosophers - St Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274)
In the Middle Ages monasteries were great centres of learning and universities such as Oxford, Paris and Bologna were being founded. Aquinas, a Dominican friar, studied in Paris, where he met Aristotle's philosophy, recently rediscovered by Arab scholars. This was a key moment because Aquinas combined Aristotle's philosophy with Christian revelation. He argued that reason can work within faith: start with faith, then use reason to reach conclusions. This was controversial then and a major shift. Like Aristotle, he held that the universe is ordered with a plan, so the search for meaning makes sense. All human actions pursue goals, and all of these are 'subgoals' of one ultimate goal. Wealth, honour, power and pleasure cannot satisfy us; only God, the complete good, can. So belief in God gives life its purpose. He wrote over eighty books, including the Summa Theologiae, and his influence is still massive today.

Key moment 2: The Age of Reason - Rene Descartes (1596-1650)
By the seventeenth century the Renaissance, the printing press and the Reformation had shaken old certainties, and scepticism was growing. Descartes, a gifted mathematician and scientist, wanted a secure foundation for philosophy. He used a 'method of doubt': reject everything that can possibly be doubted - even the senses and mathematics, in case an evil demon was tricking him. What remains must be certain. He found he could not doubt that he was doubting. Doubting is thinking, so he must exist as a thinking thing: 'I think, therefore I am.' This new confidence in the power of human reason is why he is called the 'father of modern philosophy'. The Age of Reason led on to the Enlightenment and is seen as the start of the modern age.

The Enlightenment - Rene Descartes focused on creating a secure foundation for philosophy by proving that the human mind could know things with absolute certainty by using doubt methodically; confidence in the power of reason, evident in his principle 'I think, therefore I am', is seen as inaugurating the modern age. Other valid key moments accepted. Marked 20 + 20 (20 marks for each of the two points). prompt:
In religious traditions an image of God is sometimes used to express a particular understanding of God.
Outline the ideas about God that are expressed in two traditional images of God that you have studied.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Humans use symbol and metaphor to describe God, who is beyond our full understanding. Two traditional images from the Judeo-Christian tradition are God as Father and the Creator God.

Image 1: God as Father
This image comes mainly from the New Testament. Jesus called God his father, using the intimate word 'Abba', like 'dad'. In the prayer he taught his followers (Luke 11:1-4) he began, 'Father, hallowed be your name.' The image expresses the idea that God cares for humanity as a loving parent cares for a child - protecting, guiding and nurturing. It also shows God as forgiving. In the parable of the Prodigal Son (Luke 15:11-32), the father runs to welcome home the son who wasted his inheritance, showing God's unconditional love and readiness to forgive sin. Christians are reminded that this is only one part of God's identity: God is neither man nor woman, and the male image reflects the limits of human language and the patriarchal societies where it began.

Image 2: Creator God
This image comes from the Hebrew Scriptures (Old Testament). In the Book of Genesis God creates the world and humanity and sees that it is good: 'So God created humankind in his image, in the image of God he created them; male and female he created them' (Gn 1:27). The image expresses the belief that God is eternal - he existed before creation - and all-powerful, the source of everything that exists. It links God to the beauty and diversity of nature, and it says that every human being is made in God's image and so has great dignity. Michelangelo's The Creation of Adam in the Sistine Chapel is a famous artistic expression of this image.

prompt:
Assess the reliability of the evidence for the existence of Jesus of Nazareth found in the writings of two of the following:
- An Evangelist (Matthew or Mark or Luke or John)
- Josephus
- Pliny the Younger
- Tacitus
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Source 1: Tacitus (c. 56-117 CE)
Tacitus was a Roman historian, writing around 115 CE. In The Annals he mentions Jesus when describing the burning of Rome in 64 CE. Emperor Nero blamed the Christians for the fire. Tacitus wrote that 'Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of ... Pontius Pilate', and that this 'pernicious superstition' then spread from Judea to Rome. How reliable is this? Tacitus wrote long after Jesus died, so his work is a secondary source, not an eyewitness account. However, he was hostile to Christianity and had no reason to invent Jesus. This makes his evidence strong. It confirms three facts: Jesus existed, he was executed under Pontius Pilate in the reign of Tiberius, and his movement spread to Rome.

Source 2: Josephus (c. 37-100 CE)
Josephus was a Jewish historian. He fought against Rome in the great Jewish rebellion, surrendered in 66 CE and later joined the household of the Emperors Vespasian and Titus, taking their family name, Flavius. He wrote The Jewish War and The Jewish Antiquities. In the Antiquities he mentions Jesus in the context of disturbances among the Jews under Pontius Pilate (26-36 CE). He describes Jesus as 'a wise man, a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of men who receive the truth with pleasure.' How reliable is this? Josephus wrote about sixty years after the crucifixion, so again this is not a primary source. But he was a serious historian, he was not a Christian, and he accepted both the historical reality of Jesus and the deep impact Jesus had on people.

Overall: there are no primary sources for Jesus' life, but this is normal for ancient history - there are none for Socrates either. Because Tacitus and Josephus were outsiders, and Tacitus was openly hostile, historians consider their evidence authoritative.

prompt:
Examine the impact that Jesus' resurrection had on his first disciples' understanding of him as 'Saviour' and their sense of mission.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Jesus' death was deeply shocking for his followers. They were left without their leader. Some ran away in terror, some may have lost hope and gone home, and others wondered what it had all been about. The resurrection must be understood against this background, because it completely changed them.

Understanding Jesus as Saviour
Only after the death and resurrection did the disciples begin to understand who Jesus really was. The empty tomb and the appearances - to Mary Magdalene, to Peter, to the twelve and to more than five hundred people (1 Corinthians 15) - forced them to see that Jesus was more than they had imagined. His words and actions took on a new significance. They came to see that God had been revealed in him ('Whoever has seen me has seen the Father', John 14:9). They also came to understand him as Saviour, not only of his followers but of all God's people. They used the language of ransom and redemption, taken from slavery: a slave could be redeemed if someone paid for their freedom. Jesus had paid the 'ransom' for humanity's freedom from sin and death. He was the mediator of salvation, through whom all people are reconciled to God. Early evidence of this belief is the fish symbol: the five Greek letters for 'fish' stand for 'Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour'.

A new sense of mission
The appearances reassured the disciples, reminded them of their mission and gave them instructions on how to carry on. The risen Jesus told them: 'Go, therefore, and make disciples of all nations ... I am with you always, to the end of the age' (Matthew 28:19). They knew they were no longer alone. After receiving the Spirit at Pentecost there was a dramatic change: the frightened group became bold preachers, going out to all peoples to spread the Good News. They also gained a new sense of community (Acts 2:42-47): they shared teaching, prayer and the breaking of bread, held all things in common and cared for those in need, and day by day their number grew.

So the resurrection turned fear into faith: it showed the disciples that Jesus was their Saviour and sent them out on mission.

prompt:
Outline the main features of Christian living that were emphasised by Saint Paul in his writings to one of the following first Christian communities:
- Corinth
- Philippi
- Thessalonica
(40 marks)
model_answer:
I will write about the community at Corinth.

Corinth was a wealthy seaport in the Roman Empire, a 'melting pot' of many cultures and pagan cults, with great wealth but also poverty. Paul founded the Church there on his second missionary journey in 51 CE and wrote to it in 56 CE and 57 CE. The community found the demands of this 'radical faith' - love, sharing and unity - hard to live out. In his letters Paul emphasised the following features of Christian living.

1. Unity, not loyalty to rival leaders. Members identified with particular leaders, especially the preacher Apollos, and this caused division. Paul warned them that Christians belong to one community in Christ.

2. Respect for the conscience of others. Some were scandalised by eating meat sacrificed to pagan idols; others saw no problem and looked down on them. Paul told them to follow their own conscience but be sensitive to the conscience of others: 'whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God. Give no offence ...' (1 Corinthians 10:31-33).

3. Equality and sharing, especially at worship. At their gatherings the wealthy ate and drank in abundance while the poor went without. Paul insisted that the community must include everyone, avoid divisions between rich and poor, and be generous in sharing food. He also corrected those who thought some gifts of the Spirit made them more important than others, and in his second letter he challenged their lack of generosity.

4. Belief in the resurrection. Some members did not believe in the resurrection of the dead. Paul answered that if they did not believe in the resurrection of the dead, they did not believe in the resurrection of Jesus - and that belief is a requirement of Christian faith.

Overall, Paul emphasised equality, unity and love, which were central to Jesus' message.

Thessalonica - Paul reminded Christians experiencing persecution and death about Jesus' triumph over death and future coming as Lord. prompt:
Examine the origins and purpose of inter-faith dialogue today between two of the following religions:
- Buddhism
- Christianity
- Hinduism
- Islam
- Judaism
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Inter-faith dialogue is dialogue between different faiths. I will examine dialogue between Christianity and Judaism.

Origins
Christianity grew out of Judaism. Jesus was a Jew, most of the first Christians were Jewish, and Christians and Jews share belief in one all-powerful creator God and the Hebrew Scriptures. Yet for centuries the relationship was marked by hostility and anti-Semitism, which reached its darkest point in the Holocaust, when six million Jews were murdered. In the twentieth century the world also changed: emigration brought people of many faiths to live side by side in Europe, creating multi-faith societies. People came to accept that the only way to live together is through mutual respect, co-operation and reconciliation.

Key steps followed. At the Second Vatican Council, the document Nostra Aetate stated that 'the Catholic Church rejects nothing in those religions which is true and holy', seeing in them 'a ray of that Truth which enlightens all human beings'. In 1986 Pope John Paul II visited the synagogue in Rome and called Jews 'our beloved elder brothers'. The German Bishops (1980) said that anti-Semitism is ultimately against Christ himself. Groups such as the Council of Christians and Jews were set up so members of both faiths could come together in education, dialogue and social action.

Purpose
1. To build mutual understanding: to learn about each other's beliefs and heal historic wounds. Dialogue challenges existing opinions and prejudices.
2. To foster respect and tolerance: real dialogue avoids both indifference and angry confrontation. The World Council of Churches says Christians should come 'not as manipulators but as genuine fellow-pilgrims'.
3. To share a deeper faith: dialogue distinguishes faith (the personal experience of mystery) from beliefs (its cultural expression), so people of different beliefs can share a deeper faith experience.
4. To work together for the good of all: Paul Knitter says religions must 'speak and listen to each other' and 'combine efforts for the welfare ... of all humanity', building peace and justice.

prompt:
Religious belief can inspire people at key moments in life - birth, death etc.
Outline how the influence of religious belief can be seen in the way a key moment in life is marked by members of one religion from List A and one religion from List B below:
List A: Christianity, Judaism
List B: Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The key moment I have chosen is birth.

List A: Judaism - Brit Milah
When a Jewish baby boy is eight days old he is circumcised in a ceremony called Brit Milah. This follows God's command to Abraham in Genesis 17:11-12. The circumcision is carried out by a trained Mohel, with prayers and blessings, and the child is given his name. The influence of religious belief is clear: Jews believe they are God's chosen people, bound to him by a covenant (a sacred agreement) first made with Abraham. Brit Milah is a physical sign of this Covenant between God and his people. It welcomes the child into the Jewish community and its relationship with God. Girls are named in the synagogue on the first day of Torah reading after their birth. Both rites show the Jewish belief that community and family life are central, and that each new child shares in God's promises to Israel.

List B: Islam - the Adhan and the Aqiqah
For Muslims, from birth to death life is shaped by submission to the will of Allah. As soon as a baby is born, the Adhan (the call to prayer) is recited into the baby's right ear and the Iqamah (the command to worship) into the left ear. This means the first words the child hears are about Allah and prayer, expressing the belief in one God and the hope that the child will live a life of worship. Seven days later comes the Aqiqah, the naming ceremony; a boy is also circumcised. There is usually a family feast, a customary sacrifice and almsgiving (giving to the poor). The sacrifice gives thanks to Allah for the gift of the child, and the almsgiving reflects one of the Five Pillars of Islam and the duty to care for the community. No priest is needed, because in Islam there is no priesthood: every Muslim lives by Allah's will.

prompt:
Compare the way that local communities of believers are organised within one religion from List A and one religion from List B below:
List A: Christianity, Judaism
List B: Buddhism, Hinduism, Islam
(40 marks)
model_answer:
I will compare Judaism (List A) and Buddhism (List B).

Judaism
In Judaism, community is central. It is first experienced in the home, then in festivals and Sabbath ceremonies. Most Jews belong to a local synagogue, which is led by a rabbi. The rabbi is elected by the congregation and is accountable to them. His authority comes from his learning and study of the Torah; he is not a priest who mediates God's forgiveness. He may speak for the community, but that is the limit of his authority. The community gathers regularly for worship in the synagogue, especially on the Sabbath, and also marks key life events together, such as Bar and Bat Mitzvah and weddings. A full service needs a minyan, a quorum of ten men.

Buddhism
In Buddhism the local community is organised around the Sangha, the order of monks. Monasteries are centres of learning and missionary activity, and the Sangha serves the wider community by example and teaching. Lay people support the monks by placing food in their begging bowls, and honouring the Sangha is believed to bring a better rebirth. Each monastery has a hierarchy with the abbot at its head, but real authority lies in the Buddha's teachings and precepts. Worship for lay people is largely individual, because Buddhism is a religion of self-redemption; people visit the temple or monastery at festivals or for rites, such as a naming ceremony.

Similarity
Both religions have no single central authority. Most Buddhist monasteries are independent, just as each Jewish congregation chooses its own rabbi. In both, leaders hold authority because of their learning and teaching, not because they are priests.

Difference
Jews gather as a congregation for regular communal worship on a set day (the Sabbath) in the synagogue, led by a rabbi chosen by the people. Buddhist lay people do not regularly gather together for communal worship; their worship is mostly individual, and community life centres on the monks rather than on a weekly congregation.

Christianity is different to Buddhism in that there is a parish structure in Christian Churches and believers gather together for weekly communal worship, whereas in Buddhism the local community do not regularly gather together for worship. prompt:
Using examples, discuss the role 'virtue' can play in a person's growth towards moral maturity.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Moral maturity does not appear automatically at a certain age. A morally mature person has a sense of right and wrong, thinks about how their actions affect others, can stand by their decisions even when unpopular, and has moral courage. A morally immature person is selfish, looks only for their own pleasure and follows the crowd. Virtue plays a key role in moving from one to the other.

What is virtue?
The word comes from the Greek for 'excellence'. Aristotle said a virtue is 'a kind of second nature that disposes us to do the right thing rightly'. The Catechism calls it 'a habitual and firm disposition to do the good'. A disposition is an inclination inside us that guides our actions. So virtue is about character: the more we practise and live out virtues, the more virtuous we become. Virtue ethics asks not just 'What am I doing?' but 'What sort of person am I becoming because of my actions?'

Example 1: Honesty
A student who has the virtue of honesty will tell the truth even when it causes difficulties - for example, owning up to a mistake rather than letting a friend take the blame. Each honest choice makes the next one easier, until honesty becomes part of who they are. This is moral growth: acting from settled character, not from fear of punishment.

Example 2: Courage
Courage helps a person act on what they know is right even when faced with opposition. St Thomas More lived and died by his principles, guided by courage. Mahatma Gandhi and Martin Luther King are seen as morally mature because they showed great moral courage in choosing non-violence to achieve justice for their peoples.

Example 3: Temperance
Temperance gives balance, so a person is not controlled by compulsions such as addiction to alcohol, gambling or shopping. It gives the discipline to reach true goals, like the athlete who trains hard or the student who studies for an exam.

Conclusion
Virtue gives a person the strength of character to carry out their vision for life. By building good habits, virtue helps a person move beyond selfishness and peer pressure towards the kind of principled, conscience-led living that marks true moral maturity.

The virtue of courage could guide a person to always act in a way that they know is right even when faced with opposition. Other valid points accepted. prompt:
In moral decision-making individual rights need to be balanced with 'the common good'.
Discuss the evidence for this statement making reference to an example from Irish civil law that attempts to balance individual rights with 'the common good'.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The common good is the good of the whole community - the conditions that allow everyone in society to flourish. Individual rights are the freedoms each person is entitled to. There is strong evidence that the two must be balanced.

Evidence from moral thinking
Thinkers from Aristotle and Cicero onwards held that society exists as a partnership for the common good. Christianity adds the command to love one's neighbour as oneself, which demands a commitment to the common good. The Second Vatican Council warned against selfishness and named people who ignore 'norms of social conduct such as public hygiene and speed limits' as a block to the common good. But the common good must also respect personal rights. Strict utilitarianism - doing whatever makes the majority happy - can trample on the rights of individuals, so most modern accounts insist on respecting both.

Evidence from Irish civil law
Civil law is the law a state lays down about the rights of its people. Personal rights are protected in Articles 40-44 of the Irish Constitution, but they are not absolute. When the Constitution was debated in 1937, Eamon de Valera said the rights of the individual and of the community must 'not conflict and properly coordinate'.

Example: speed limits and drink-driving laws. Every adult has the right to own a car and drive. But Irish law sets speed limits and limits on drinking and driving. These restrict individual freedom in order to protect the common good - the safety of all road users - by preventing dangerous driving. Most people accept this balance because a dangerous driver threatens other people's right to life.

Irish courts have also weighed these values. In the Murray case, two prisoners serving life sentences claimed a constitutional right to have children. The Supreme Court ruled that this right was subservient to the common good of protecting the community from dangerous criminals. In the Derrynaflan Hoard case, the Court found that the State's right to own national treasure outweighed the rights of the finders.

Conclusion
The evidence shows that neither side can be absolute. As the Irish proverb says, people live in each other's shelter: the law must protect each person's rights, but sometimes limit them so that everyone can live safely together.

An excellent answer shows knowledge of communal values by examining and drawing accurate conclusions about how an example from Irish civil law tries to balance individual rights with what is regarded as best for society as a whole. A State's duty to protect the health of the nation has to be held in balance with the right of people to choose how they live their lives, e.g. Covid-19 restrictions limiting the distance people can travel and requiring face coverings limit individual freedom to ensure that the 'common good' of all people in society is protected. Other valid examples accepted. Marked as one 40-mark answer, graded on four criteria: evidence of the marking criteria, relevance, use of skill, factual accuracy. prompt:
Profile how there has been a change in thinking, since the Enlightenment, about the morality of two of the following issues:
- Capital Punishment
- Child Labour
- Slavery
- War
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The Enlightenment (the eighteenth century, around the time of the French Revolution) broke with ancient and medieval thought and put new trust in human reason and science. Ideas that began then, such as democratic government and human rights, are now accepted by almost everyone, including the churches. These ideas changed moral thinking on many issues.

Issue 1: Capital punishment
Before: Christian ethics has not always opposed the death penalty. In the Law of Moses fifteen crimes carried the death penalty, and it was long held to be the State's duty to punish the gravest crimes in this way.
Change: The Enlightenment brought trust in evidence and the scientific method, and new human sciences such as sociology and psychology. Research has shown that the death penalty does not reduce violent crime, so it has no real value as a deterrent. Other problems became clear: an innocent person who is executed cannot be put right, and in the USA a disproportionate number of people from minority ethnic groups are on death row. Church teaching moved too. Pope John Paul II, in Evangelium Vitae, said the death penalty could be justified only if there were no other way to protect society, and such cases are 'rare, if not non-existent'. The clear movement now is that human dignity always stays with a person, whatever they have done, and the focus has shifted towards rehabilitation and reform.

Issue 2: Slavery
Before: Slavery was part of life in biblical times and seemed acceptable to the New Testament writers. Even Thomas Jefferson, a leading Enlightenment figure in America, owned African American slaves.
Change: Enlightenment ideas about equality and human rights led to a new understanding that every person's freedom must be respected. Only in the last two centuries has slavery become illegal and widely seen as against human dignity. Today people are protected by international human rights law. This growing respect for the dignity of every individual also makes us aware of modern forms of slavery, such as child labour in factories, human trafficking and child soldiers, which are now condemned.
marking_scheme: Skill: profiling (accurately tracing). An excellent answer shows an understanding of morality as a human phenomenon by accurately tracing how the understanding of right and wrong in two of the issues listed has changed since the time of the Enlightenment. Points of reference, e.g.: Capital Punishment - ideas about using evidence, scientific method etc.; social science research, showing how capital punishment does not always have a deterrent effect, changed people's thinking and promoted the greater benefits of rehabilitation and reform. Child Labour - Enlightenment ideas about human rights led to a new understanding of the rights of children and of workers; limits were placed on the types of work children could do; today children are protected under the UN rights of the child. Slavery - ideas about equality led to a new understanding that every person's freedom has to be respected; slavery came to be understood as morally wrong; people today are protected against slavery by the UN Charter of Human Rights. War - ideas about human rights and democracy strengthened the principles of the 'Just War' theory, whereby a war must have very specific grounds to be considered 'just'; this gave weight to ideas about the 'rightful ruler' and the proportionality argument. Note: allow descriptive answers. Marked 20 + 20 (20 marks for each of the two points). Each half is graded on four criteria: evidence of the marking criteria, relevance, use of skill, factual accuracy. prompt:
Outline how two myths, from ancient cultures, attempted to answer key questions about the meaning of life.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
A myth is a symbolic story, passed down by word of mouth, that tries to explain why things are the way they are. Myths came before philosophy and science, so they are the earliest evidence of humanity's search for meaning.

Myth 1: Prometheus (Ancient Greece). This myth, first recorded in Greece in the late eighth century BCE, tries to answer the questions 'Where did fire come from?' and 'Why is there suffering?'. Zeus, the most powerful god, was angry with humans and took away their fire. Prometheus, who acts as a go-between for gods and humans, crept into Olympus, lit a torch from the Sun and smuggled glowing charcoal out in a fennel stalk to give fire to mankind. Zeus took revenge: Prometheus was chained to a pillar while an eagle tore at his liver every day. Zeus also had Pandora made. She opened a jar that let out all the Spites that plague humans - Old Age, Labour, Sickness, Insanity, Vice and Passion. So the myth explains that suffering came into the world through the anger of the gods. It also answers questions about good and evil (Prometheus is good, defending humanity; Zeus is a vengeful god to be feared) and about hope, which was also shut in the jar.

Myth 2: Gilgamesh (Mesopotamia, modern Iraq). This myth tries to answer 'Why do we die?' and 'Is there eternal life?'. After the death of his friend Enkidu, King Gilgamesh set out to find the secret of eternal life. The goddess told him to stop and enjoy the ordinary joys of life, because when the gods created man 'they put death upon mankind'. He went on, met Utnapishtim, and dived to the bottom of the cosmic sea to pick a plant that gives back youth. But on the way home a serpent ate the plant and shed its skin, and Gilgamesh wept. The myth answers that death is part of being human, and it also explains why snakes shed their skin. Its sad ending shows that people long ago feared death and searched for meaning in the face of it.

prompt:
Compare how a key question about life is treated in an ancient myth with the way it is answered from a scientific point of view today.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The key question I will compare is: 'How did the universe begin?'

In the ancient myth: The Genesis creation account comes from the Jewish people. It says that one God is responsible for all of creation. God creates the world in six days and rests on the seventh. Like other myths, it is a symbolic story. It was not written to give scientific facts. It answers the deeper questions: Who made the world? Why is it here? Does it have a purpose? Its answer is that the world is good, that it comes from God, and that humans are made in God's image.

In modern science: The Big Bang theory, developed by George Lemaitre (a Catholic priest), says the universe exploded into existence about 13.8 billion years ago from a tiny beginning. It is supported by evidence. The second law of thermodynamics says the universe becomes more disordered every day, so it cannot have existed forever. In the 1920s Edwin Hubble found that the galaxies are moving apart, so the universe must once have been smaller. Heat radiating from space is thought to be heat left over from the Big Bang.

Similarities: Both say the universe had a beginning - it has not always been there. Both see a creation event. Both try to explain our place in the universe.

Differences: The myth answers 'who' and 'why' through a symbolic story; science answers 'how' and 'when' using measurement, reason and testing. The myth says God is the cause; science has not yet found the cause of creation. The myth's time-scale is six days; science speaks of billions of years. The myth gives the world a purpose; science alone does not, and its prediction that the universe will one day die (Big Chill or Big Crunch) can make people ask how life can be meaningful.

prompt:

Explain how the understanding of God/gods/the transcendent in two of the above religions influences the way sacred texts are interpreted by their members today.

Transcendent means beyond normal human experience. In religion it is another word for God. Both Christianity and Islam believe God is transcendent, but they understand God differently, and this shapes how they read their sacred texts.

Christianity: Christians believe God is a mystery beyond us (the Trinity - three persons in one God) and yet close to us. The high point of this is the Incarnation: Jesus, the Second Person of the Trinity, became fully human while staying fully divine. John's Gospel calls him 'the Word made flesh' (John 1:14). Because of this, Christians read the Bible as the word of God, but they see Jesus himself as the fullness of God's revelation. The Old Testament is read as God's revelation building up to Jesus, and the Gospels are read to come to know Jesus. Christians also believe God is still revealing himself through the Holy Spirit, so the Bible is interpreted with the help of Tradition and the Church community. For Christians today the Bible is a source of comfort, challenge and inspiration, and a Gospel is read at every Sacrament.

Islam: Muslims believe Allah is the absolute 'other', totally one and beyond understanding. Nothing can be compared to him, so there are no images of Allah in mosques. They believe Allah revealed himself for the final time to the Prophet Muhammad, through the angel Jibril, and that the Qur'an contains Allah's own words, not just a message about him. Because of this, the Qur'an is treated with the greatest respect. It is seen as complete and final, so it is not open to change or criticism, and it is preserved in its original Arabic. Muslims recite it in daily prayer and feel close to Allah through its words. Its teaching is also the basis of the Sharia, which the ulama interpret to guide the community today.

prompt:
Imagine you had a chance to talk with Anselm and Aquinas about their understanding of God.
Outline what you think each would say about how belief in the existence of God could help a person searching for the meaning of life today.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
St Anselm (1033-1109): 'I was Archbishop of Canterbury and I started from faith - I believed in God and wanted to understand that belief. By the word God we mean the greatest being that can be imagined. Now, something that exists in reality is greater than something that only exists in the mind. So if God only existed in the mind, he would not be the greatest being. Therefore God must exist in reality. This is now called the ontological argument. For a person searching for meaning today, this tells them that there is a perfect being, greater than anything we can think of. Your life is not an accident in an empty universe. If God is perfect goodness and love, then your life can have a purpose - to grow towards that goodness. Your longing for something greater is itself a sign that God is real.'

St Thomas Aquinas (1225-1274): 'I lived at a time when reason was admired, and I wanted to show that faith is reasonable. I gave five proofs. Nothing moves itself, so there must be a first mover. Nothing creates itself, so there must be an uncreated creator - the first cause. Everything depends on something else, so there must be a necessary being. We see degrees of beauty and goodness, so there must be a perfect standard. The universe is ordered, so it must be directed by a supreme intelligence. That is God. The world does not explain itself - its existence, its order and its beauty point beyond it to God, its origin and goal. For someone searching today, this means the world makes sense: it comes from God and is going towards God. The restlessness you feel, as St Augustine said, is because "our hearts are restless until they rest in you". Belief in God gives you a reason for living and a direction for your life.'

prompt:
Outline how each of the following were affected by Roman rule in Palestine, during Jesus of Nazareth's lifetime:
- Political System
- Religious System
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Political system: The Romans colonised Palestine in 63 BCE. At first they ruled through native kings, such as Herod the Great, who was king when Jesus was born. After his death in 4 BCE his kingdom was split between his sons. Herod Archelaus ruled Judea so badly that Rome removed him and began direct rule. Judea became a Roman province governed by a prefect appointed by the Emperor. In Jesus' time this was Pontius Pilate. Galilee, where Jesus lived, was ruled by Herod Antipas, a 'puppet' prince who took orders from Rome and collected Roman taxes. So the real power lay with a foreign Emperor. Taxes were a huge problem: Jews believed the land belonged to God, so paying taxes to Caesar felt like being unfaithful to God. This led to tension and unrest, especially in Galilee, and the prefect watched large gatherings in Jerusalem closely.

Religious system: Rome was polytheistic and the Emperor was treated as a god. This was in direct conflict with Jewish monotheism - belief in Yahweh alone - and threatened Jewish identity. The high priest was Head of State and led the Sanhedrin, the 71-member High Council, but he had little real power: the Roman prefect could appoint and dismiss him. The Sadducees, linked to the Temple, were the most powerful group in the Sanhedrin and co-operated with Rome to keep their power. Roman rule also caused Jewish groups to respond in different ways: the Zealots used violent resistance; the Pharisees kept strict observance of the Law, such as the Sabbath, to protect Jewish identity; and the Essenes withdrew. The Temple in Jerusalem remained the centre of religious life, but it was under the shadow of Rome.

prompt:
Describe how Jesus of Nazareth's words and actions showed an awareness of what was involved in two of the following Jewish expectations of the Messiah:
- Davidic
- Priestly
- Prophetic
(40 marks)
model_answer:
'Messiah' means 'anointed one'. In times of hardship the Jews hoped God would send a messiah to save them.

Davidic Messiah: This was the general popular hope - a new King David who would begin a new era and free the Jews from the Romans, like a military leader. Jesus showed he knew of this hope. The genealogies in Matthew and Luke trace his family back through David. After the miracle of the loaves and fish the people wanted to make him king, but Jesus went away. He would not be a political or warrior king. Instead he taught in Mark 8:31 that the Son of Man 'must undergo great suffering, and be rejected... and be killed, and after three days rise again'. He was aware of the Davidic hope but changed it: his Kingdom of God would come through love, service and his own death, not through war against Rome. This is why he was careful not to be called Messiah in a political sense.

Prophetic Messiah: The Pharisees hoped for a messiah who would fulfil the scriptures and free God's people from oppression, as Moses freed the Israelites from slavery in Egypt. Jesus does show some closeness to this idea. In the Sermon on the Mount he is like a new Moses giving God's law, but he makes it internal: 'You have heard that it was said... But I say to you...'. He calls for a change of heart based on love. After his baptism he goes out on a mission, like a prophet's call, and the crowds said 'God has visited his people' (Luke 7:16). At the well he told the Samaritan woman, 'I am he' (John 4:26). But his idea of freedom was freedom from sin and a Kingdom of love for all, which was very different from what the Pharisees expected.

prompt:
Describe two examples of what has been achieved in the search for unity between Christian Churches today.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The ecumenical movement is the effort to heal divisions between Christian Churches. The word comes from the Greek 'oikoumene', meaning 'the whole world'. It focuses on what Churches share - faith in Jesus Christ - and aims at reconciliation and respect, not one uniform Church.

Example 1: The Week of Prayer for Christian Unity. In 1908 two Anglicans began the Church Unity Octave, a week of prayer for unity. Today Christian Unity Week is held every January, usually 18th-25th. Catholics, Protestants and Orthodox Christians hold joint prayer services in each other's churches. This was helped by the Second Vatican Council, whose document on ecumenism recognised the work of the Holy Spirit in other Christian Churches. It is a real achievement because for centuries the Churches stressed their differences. Praying together shows Jesus' own prayer 'that they may all be one' being put into practice.

Example 2: Working for peace in Ireland. Christianity has a dark side: sectarianism in Northern Ireland divided communities. In response, the Irish Council of Churches and the Catholic Commission for Justice and Peace have worked together through an Inter-Church Committee and peace education programmes for schools. The Corrymeela Community, set up in 1965 by Presbyterian chaplain Ray Davey, brings Protestants and Catholics together to break down barriers. Billy Kane of Corrymeela said living in segregated communities and hating each other is 'not normal'. These achievements follow the mission of Jesus, who promoted peace instead of violence.

Other signs of progress include Taize in France, where many denominations pray together, and One Bread One Body (1998), which says 'we preach the same Christ'. Difficulties remain, such as different views on the Eucharist, but the Churches stay committed to dialogue.

prompt:
Profile how Jesus of Nazareth's words and actions are remembered in two ceremonies that are part of Christian worship today.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Ceremony 1: The Eucharist (the Mass). At the Last Supper, a Passover meal, Jesus took bread and the cup and said, 'This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me' (Luke 22:19). The apostles kept this command - Acts 2:42-47 describes the early Christians 'breaking bread' together. Today, at every Eucharist, the priest repeats Jesus' words over the bread and wine. For Catholics, 'memorial' is at the heart of the Eucharistic prayer: it is 'the making effective in the present of an event in the past'. Christ's gift of his life for our salvation is made present, and Catholics believe Christ is truly present in the bread and wine (transubstantiation). Protestants focus on remembering the Last Supper and see the bread and wine as symbols of Christ's presence. The Gospel readings recall Jesus' words and actions. Remembering also means living as Jesus did - he washed his disciples' feet and said, 'you also ought to wash one another's feet' (John 13:14).

Ceremony 2: Baptism. Jesus was baptised in the river Jordan, and he commanded his followers to baptise all nations (Matthew 28). Baptism initiates a person into Christianity. The word 'baptise' means 'to plunge'. In the rite, a prayer recalls that Jesus overcame evil, and the person is anointed with the oil of salvation, naming Christ 'our saviour'. The water is blessed, recalling the blood and water that flowed from Jesus' side on the cross. Being plunged into the water symbolises being buried with Christ in his death and rising with him as 'a new creature'. A final anointing points to everlasting life. Parents and godparents promise to raise the child in the faith. In this way Jesus' death and resurrection are remembered and shared by each new Christian.

prompt:
Examine how the relationship between the 'sacred' and 'profane' aspects of life can be communicated through the role individual people play within a religion.

The sacred is what is 'set aside for religious use' - the things of God. The profane is 'the world of everyday existence, the ordinary and mundane'. Example 1: The shaman in primal religions. A shaman is a tribal elder or holy person who is a living mediator between the human world and the spirit world. The gift is usually inherited from ancestors. The shaman journeys into the spirit world to gain prophetic wisdom and knowledge of medicine, and then brings this back to heal people physically and spiritually. The shaman is said to be 'seized by the Divine'. Looking closely, the shaman's role shows that for primal peoples the sacred and profane are not separate: the spirit world directly affects everyday matters like sickness, food and protection. The shaman stands at the boundary and carries the power of the sacred into ordinary life. Even today, people still look to shamans for advice.

Example 2: The ulama and imam in Islam. Islam has no priesthood, so there is no one who stands between the believer and Allah. The imam is a teacher and community leader, not an ordained priest, and any faithful Muslim can lead prayer. This role shows a different relationship: in Islam the sacred is not kept apart from daily life. Through the ulama's guidance, ordinary actions such as business, eating and family life become acts of obedience to Allah.

prompt:
Compare the way that the community of believers is structured and organised in one religion from LIST A and one religion from LIST B below:

I will compare Judaism (List A) and Islam (List B).

Judaism: Community is central in Judaism. It is first experienced in the home, then in festivals and the Sabbath. Most Jews belong to a local synagogue led by a rabbi. The rabbi is elected by the congregation and is accountable to them. His authority comes from his learning and study of the Torah, not from being a go-between with God. A full service needs a minyan of ten men. The weekly Sabbath (Shabbat) is a day of rest, worship and family. Key life events, such as Bar Mitzvah and Bat Mitzvah, are celebrated by the community. prompt:
Outline the origins of the relationship between Christianity and Judaism using each of the following headings:

Christianity grew out of Judaism. Jesus was a Jew, and most of the first Christians were Jewish. Their worship, prayer and organisation were the foundation of Church practice. Christians share the Hebrew Bible (the Old Testament) with Jews.

Jews accept God's offer of salvation by keeping the commandments (mitzvot) with loving obedience, and even sinners can repent and return (teshuvah). The Jews also hoped God would send a messiah, an 'anointed one', to save them. Christianity's vision of salvation began from these same roots. Both faiths see love of God and love of neighbour as inseparable, and both stress the holiness of creation.

A Celebrating Tradition: Judaism is a celebrating tradition with weekly and yearly festivals. The Sabbath is a weekly day of rest and worship. Passover (Pesach) celebrates God freeing the people from slavery in Egypt, with the Seder meal at home. Shavuot (Pentecost), fifty days after Passover, celebrates the giving of the Law to Moses. Christian celebration grew from these. The Last Supper was a Passover meal, so the Eucharist has its roots in Passover. Fixed times of daily prayer have Jewish roots, the Psalms are prayed by both, and Hebrew words like 'Amen' and 'Alleluia' are still used by Christians.

'Morality is so deeply rooted in our everyday lives that it seems hard to imagine a society without any moral rules.'

prompt:
Outline what is involved in two stages of personal moral development put forward by a moral theorist that you have studied.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The moral theorist I have studied is Lawrence Kohlberg. He applied Piaget's ideas to moral development. He gave children moral dilemmas and studied how they reasoned. He said there are three levels, each with two stages, and that we must pass through the stages in order. Each stage is more complex than the one before.

Stage 1: Obedience-Punishment Orientation (Level I, Pre-conventional, roughly age 4-10). At this level the moral value lies in the person's own needs and wants. In Stage 1 a moral decision is driven by the need to avoid punishment. Right is whatever does not get me into trouble; wrong is whatever gets me punished. For example, little Hugh will not hit his sister because he does not want to get shouted at. He is not thinking about his sister's feelings, only about the consequences for himself. Kohlberg said adults can still act at this stage - for example, a soldier carrying out an atrocity in war to avoid being killed himself.

Stage 4: Law and Order Orientation (Level II, Conventional, roughly age 10-13). At this level the moral value lies in keeping the conventional order and pleasing others. In Stage 4 a moral decision is driven by the need not to be criticised by an authority figure. The person respects law, order and authority in general and has a strong sense of duty to the social order. Justice is seen as punishment for breaking the law. For example, careful Hugh will not smoke in school because it is against the rules.

Kohlberg believed the morally mature person reaches the post-conventional level, guided by principles and conscience. Carol Gilligan criticised him, saying his higher stages are biased toward male ways of thinking.

prompt:
Trace how the influence of the Covenant and the Decalogue can be seen in two examples of Jesus of Nazareth's preaching.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The Covenant is the bond God made with Israel - with Abraham and with Moses at Sinai. It came from God's love, not from anything the people earned. The Decalogue (Ten Commandments, Exodus 20 and Deuteronomy 5) is the people's way of responding to that love. The commandments are followed as a unit: the first three are about love of God and the last seven about love of neighbour.

Example 1: The Commandment of Love. When asked 'Which commandment is the first of all?', Jesus answered with the Shema: 'Hear, O Israel: the Lord our God, the Lord is one; you shall love the Lord your God with all your heart...', and added 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself' (Mark 12:28-34, quoting Deuteronomy 6 and Leviticus 19). This is a short summary of the Decalogue: love of God sums up the first three commands, and love of neighbour sums up the other seven. It also shows the Covenant idea that the law is a loving response to a loving God. At the Last Supper Jesus washed his disciples' feet as an example of unconditional love and gave a 'new commandment': 'love one another. Just as I have loved you' (John 13:34).

Example 2: The Sermon on the Mount (Matthew 5-7). Matthew wrote for a Jewish community and shows Jesus as deepening the Old Law, not abolishing it. Jesus uses the pattern 'You have heard that it was said... But I say to you...'. For example, the commandment 'You shall not kill' becomes a call not even to hold anger or hatred in your heart. Like the command 'You shall not covet', this makes morality internal - it is about our motives. The Catechism says the Sermon 'releases [the] hidden potential' of the Old Law. Jesus also told the rich young man to 'keep the commandments', listing them, but then called him to go further and follow him.

prompt:
Imagine Plato was giving a talk about the nature of reality for people today.
From your knowledge of Plato's ideas about the nature of reality outline one point that you think he would emphasise for people today.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
One point Plato would emphasise for people today is that the world we see with our senses is not the most real world. Plato believed that true knowledge comes through the mind alone, not through the physical senses, because the senses can deceive us. In his Theory of Ideal Forms, everything in our world takes its qualities from an 'ideal form' that exists on its own. For example, every chair we see shares in the ideal form of 'chair-ness'. The ideal form is more real than the physical object because it never changes, wears away or is destroyed. Truth, beauty, goodness and justice are unchanging ideal forms.
Plato explained this in the Allegory of the Cave. Prisoners are chained facing a wall and see only shadows cast by a fire. They think the shadows are real. When one prisoner is freed, he is dazzled by the fire and then the sun, but he comes to see the truth. When he returns to tell the others, they do not believe him. For Plato, our physical world of change, ageing and decay is the world of shadows. The sun stands for the ultimate ideal form, the Good. So his point for people today would be: do not mistake appearances for reality; use your reason to search for what is truly real and lasting.

prompt:

model_answer:
Plato would emphasise that the physical world is not the most real world because many people today live as if appearances are everything. Plato saw the world of material objects as always changing and so only a shadow of what is real. Today people are surrounded by images on screens and social media, by advertising and by the latest products. Like the prisoners in the cave, people can take these shadows for reality and never look further. Plato would want them to turn away from what is on the surface and use their minds to search for lasting truth.
He would also stress this because he believed true happiness comes from wisdom, not from pleasure alone. In the Philebus, Socrates says that pure pleasure without thought suits only an oyster, and that the highest good is wisdom. Plato wanted a sensible mix of pleasure and wisdom, led by knowledge and reason. In his allegory of the chariot, reason (the charioteer) must guide our appetites and our spirit together towards a goal. Many people today chase short-term pleasures that do not satisfy. Plato would say that by looking beyond appearances to the Good, and by living with wisdom and virtue, people can find real meaning and happiness.

prompt:
Outline a key idea that was taught by one person associated with the development of the humanist tradition.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Desiderius Erasmus (1466-1536) was a great Renaissance humanist. He was born in Rotterdam, became an Augustinian monk and was ordained a priest in 1492. He was a devout Christian, but he was critical of the Church and called for spiritual renewal in the Church and society.
His key idea was the power of education. Erasmus believed in the dignity of the human person, and he believed that education is how humans improve and excel. He said, 'People are not born, but formed.' For Erasmus, education trains the mind, helps a person's moral and spiritual development and promotes civic virtues. He stressed the importance of the teacher and of good teaching methods, and he believed every person has an inborn ability to reach perfection. Parents and teachers have a duty to help children reach their potential. Without education, he said, humans have no humanity, because education raises us above the beasts. A well-educated child would grow into 'a faithful protector of his family ... and a solid and useful citizen of his country'. Erasmus was a Christian humanist: he encouraged people to question the issues of the day, but he did not question scripture, and he held up Jesus Christ as the model of the human person.

prompt:
Using examples, trace how the religious practice of believers is influenced by the understanding of divine revelation in two major world religions that you have studied.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Christianity: Christians believe God revealed himself through creation and the history of the Jewish people, and that Jesus Christ is the high point of revelation. John 1:14 says, 'The Word became flesh and lived among us.' Jesus is God's most complete self-communication. This shapes Christian practice. Because Jesus is the fullness of revelation, Christians gather to celebrate the Eucharist, where they remember his words and actions at the Last Supper. At the Eucharist they say the Nicene Creed, 'I believe in One God', which sums up God's revelation in sending his Son. A Gospel reading is part of the ritual of each Sacrament, showing belief that Jesus is the Son of God. Belief in God as Trinity, revealed in Matthew 28:19, is expressed every time a Christian makes the sign of the cross: 'In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.' Christians also pray the Rosary, reflecting on the mysteries of God revealed in the life of Jesus.
Islam: Muslims believe Allah revealed himself for the last time in the seventh century to the Prophet Muhammad. This revelation is contained in the Qur'an, which holds God's own words and is the complete and final guidance for humanity. Because the Qur'an reveals that there is only one God, Muslims repeat the Shahada many times each day. Because they must submit to Allah's will, they pray (Salat) five times a day. Because Muhammad is God's messenger, Mecca, his home town, is the focus of daily prayer and of the Hajj, whose rituals recall Muhammad and Abraham. Because Allah is a transcendent mystery beyond understanding, there are no images of Allah, Muhammad, humans or animals in mosques, to avoid idolatry. In both religions, what believers think God has revealed directly shapes how they pray and worship.

prompt:
Explain two reasons why people could become indifferent to the search for the meaning of life in the world today.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Indifference is a sense that the search for meaning is irrelevant or cannot be reached. Viktor Frankl called this the 'existential vacuum'. Two reasons why people could become indifferent are consumerism and pessimism.
1. Consumerism: We are bombarded with advertising that promises happiness if we buy a product, drive a certain car or wear certain clothes. This is the 'logic of the marketplace', where everything has a price and a shelf life. It puts short-term happiness ahead of lasting meaning and leaves little room to reflect on big questions. But material things do not satisfy for long. Studies of lotto winners show they return to about their original level of happiness within a year; this is called hedonic adaptation. A new phone gives a quick thrill, but soon we want a newer one, so the consumer never fully arrives. If people keep chasing the next purchase, they may never stop to ask what life is really for, and so become indifferent to the search for meaning.
2. Pessimism: Some people become indifferent to all values and beliefs. This can hide anger or deep pessimism and leave a sense of emptiness. It can come from illness, unemployment, the breakdown of a relationship, grief or loneliness. Recent events such as the Covid-19 pandemic, war in Ukraine and economic crisis could add to this feeling. The attitude becomes 'so what?' - there is nothing to believe in and no one to believe in. It may also come from the loss of the community and social ties that once anchored people's lives. A person who feels this way may decide that searching for meaning is pointless, and stop searching altogether.

prompt:
Describe two examples of the different ways that Jesus of Nazareth taught his followers about the Kingdom of God through his words and actions.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
1. Words - the parables: A parable is a story drawn from ordinary everyday life with a religious or moral lesson, meant to bring the hearer to decision or action. Jesus was a master of the parable. His characters were farmers, shepherds, women cleaning houses, fathers and sons, so his listeners could see themselves in the stories. The parables often surprised people. In the Workers in the Vineyard (Matthew 20:1-16), those who work one hour get the same pay as those who work all day. In the Lost Son (Luke 15:11-32), the father welcomes home the son who wasted everything. Through these stories Jesus called his listeners to metanoia - repentance and a change of heart. He invited them to choose peace over violence, to include rather than exclude, to share rather than hoard, and to know God as a loving God. These are the marks of the Kingdom, where 'the last will be first, and the first will be last'.
2. Actions - the miracles: In biblical times illness was seen as a punishment for sin and a sign of God's displeasure. Jesus showed the opposite through his healing miracles: a blind man sees (Matthew 9:27-30), a leper is cured (Matthew 8:1-3), and a woman bent low stands up straight (Luke 13:11-13). These actions taught that God cares for and loves those who suffer, and that in the Kingdom the sick are healed and those on the edge are included. Other miracles taught more about the Kingdom: the loaves and fishes show there is plenty for all; the calming of the storm shows there is no need to be afraid; and the raising of Lazarus shows that death has no power over God. Through these great deeds Jesus showed that God's Kingdom was already breaking into the world.

prompt:
Profile how one Christian denomination is trying to carry on the mission of Jesus through their work in the world today.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The Roman Catholic Church tries to carry on the mission of Jesus through its work for justice, especially for the poor.
Jesus' mission: Jesus announced the Kingdom of God, where justice would rule and all would be included. He allied himself with the poor, the sick, the widowed and those despised by society. St Paul summed up this vision in Galatians 3:28: 'There is no longer Jew or Greek, there is no longer slave or free, there is no longer male or female; for all of you are one in Christ Jesus.' In Christ all are equal, with no discrimination by race, religion, class or gender.
How the Catholic Church continues this mission: Catholics believe that through baptism they have a duty to work for justice. The Church has adopted the 'option for the poor', which came from the liberation theologians of Latin America. It means the Christian call to stand in solidarity with the poor and oppressed, just as Jesus did.
Trócaire: Trócaire is the overseas development agency of the Catholic Church in Ireland. It carries on Jesus' mission by working against poverty and injustice around the world. For example, Trócaire has identified forms of modern slavery: bonded labour, forced labour, trafficking, chattel slavery and the worst forms of child labour. One case is Kyi Win, a twelve-year-old boy forced by Burma's military rulers to work unpaid on a railway, who was kicked in the face by a soldier when he paused. By speaking out about such cases and supporting the poor, the Church follows Jesus, who challenged the real injustice of slavery in his time.
Other Catholic work: groups such as the St Vincent de Paul Society help poor families in Ireland. The Church also teaches care for the earth's resources, following Jesus' concern for 'wholeness and shalom for all creatures'. In all of this, the Catholic Church tries to make the Kingdom of justice, compassion and inclusion that Jesus preached a reality today.

prompt:
Trace how the influence of two ideas associated with primal religion can be seen in a major world religion that you have studied.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Major world religion: Christianity.
1. Tabu (sacred things set apart): In primal religions, tabu was any person, object or place 'set apart' from everyday use and consecrated for ritual and worship. Sacred objects could only be handled by people who were ritually pure, and rules of washing and purification kept them separate. This idea can be seen in Christianity, where churches are consecrated as sacred spaces and certain objects, such as the chalice and the tabernacle, are kept only for worship. Christians still use rituals of washing and blessing, for example blessing themselves with holy water as they enter a church.
2. A sacred natural world: Primal peoples lived close to nature and saw no boundary between the sacred and everyday life; religion was part of all of life. In Ireland this can be seen in Celtic Christianity. St Patrick and the Celtic saints adapted pre-Christian practices into the Christian faith, for example holy wells and the pilgrimage to Croagh Patrick. Celtic Christianity saw God's presence in all of nature and held the sacred and the everyday together, just as primal religion did.

prompt:
The number of different religions in Ireland has increased in recent years.
Describe another trend within religion in Ireland that has emerged in recent years.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Trend: secularisation.
Secularisation is a movement in culture that focuses on nature and science and their benefits to humankind. A secularised society shows a declining interest in religion, and religious structures have little influence on ethical, economic or social thinking. Causes of change in Ireland include rising wealth and education, scientific and technological progress, and challenges to traditional authority.
Eoin G. Cassidy studied religion in Ireland between 1980 and 2000 using the European Values Study. He found that the number of Irish people who could be called 'secularists' rose from 2.5 per cent in 1981 to 8 per cent in 1999. Belief in God stayed high at 96 per cent, so he concluded that Ireland was resisting secularisation. However, he found a decline in following Catholic moral teaching on issues such as abortion, sex before marriage and same-sex relationships, which suggests 'the influence of a secularist ethos'. Church influence was weakest among young adults. More recently, the referendums on same-sex marriage and abortion showed that many people are now less influenced by Church teaching on moral issues. So, while many Irish people still believe in God, religion has less influence on how people make moral and social decisions.

Religions chosen: Judaism (List A) and Islam (List B).
Judaism - Passover (Pesach): Judaism's founding story includes God's covenant with Abraham and the Exodus, when Moses led the Israelites out of about four hundred years of slavery in Egypt. Passover is one of the three major 'foot' festivals and lasts eight days. It celebrates God freeing his people from Egypt. The heart of the festival is the Seder, a special meal in the home. The Haggadah, the story of the Exodus, is read aloud. Children take an active part by asking, 'Why is this night different from all other nights?' The most important symbolic food is matzah, unleavened bread, which recalls the hurried escape from Egypt.
Islam - Eid-ul-Adha: Islam is rooted in the faith of Abraham. Eid-ul-Adha, the Festival of Sacrifice, lasts four days and is the climax of the Hajj and the major festival of the Muslim year. It recalls Abraham's complete submission to God when he was willing to sacrifice his son. This is an example for Muslims, since 'Islam' means submission. Rituals include sacrifice, charity, feasting, visiting cemeteries, exchanging gifts, wearing new clothes and visiting family.
Similarities: Both festivals recall a founding event in which God acts in the lives of his people, and both trace back to Abraham. Both are celebrated with a special festive meal shared with family, and both use food as a symbol of the story.
Differences: Passover recalls a story of freedom - God rescuing a whole people from slavery - while Eid-ul-Adha recalls a story of one man's submission and willingness to sacrifice. Passover is mainly celebrated at home through retelling the story at the Seder, while Eid-ul-Adha is linked to the pilgrimage to Mecca and is marked by sacrifice and giving to the poor. The festivals also follow different calendars: Passover follows the Hebrew calendar, while Eid follows the Islamic lunar calendar, so it moves through the seasons.

prompt:

Conflict situation: Israel and the Palestinians.
Background: In 135 CE the Romans drove the Jews out of Jerusalem and named the area Palestine. Muslim Arab armies later conquered the region and Muslims stayed in control until the early twentieth century. Jerusalem became holy to Muslims because, according to the Qur'an, Muhammad ascended to heaven from there, and the Al Aqsa Mosque was built on the area seen as the site of the old Jewish Temple. Role of religion: For both Jews and Muslims, religious identity is tied up with ideas of homeland and claims over land. Many Jews believe the land was promised to Abraham, while Muslims also see it as sacred. So, while the conflict is also political, religion is part of the problem - and can be part of the solution.

- It builds understanding. Dialogue is a challenging encounter that questions existing opinions and prejudices. If Jews and Muslims meet and learn about each other's beliefs, suspicion and misunderstanding can be reduced.
- It finds common ground. Both faiths trace their roots to Abraham, and both teach a version of the Golden Rule. Judaism says, 'What is hateful to you, do not do to your fellow human being', and Islam says, 'No one of you is a believer until he desires for his brother that which he desires for himself.' Dialogue can remind both sides of these shared values.
- It gives good examples. In 1986 Pope John Paul II prayed at Assisi with Jews, Muslims, Hindus and Buddhists. Paolo Dall'Oglio founded the community of Deir Mar Musa in Syria to build respect between Muslims and Christians, saying 'we cannot continue to use religion as an excuse for violence of all kinds.'

prompt:
Describe an example of the moral issues that were a concern for people living in each of the following ancient civilisations:
- The Hebrews
- The Romans
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The Hebrews - freedom: For the Hebrews, morality was part of their relationship with God, shaped by the Torah and the Covenant. Freedom was one of the great moral concerns. It has been valued since the Exodus, when God freed the Hebrews from slavery in Egypt so that they could live as his people and serve him. Being free to devote their lives to God was a real issue whenever they were oppressed or occupied by foreign powers, and continual persecution down through history has made freedom even more important. It also includes personal freedom - the right to shape one's own destiny. Linked to this was a passion for justice. The prophets and psalms condemned personal and social injustice as sinful. God was seen as caring for the powerless - the widow, the orphan and the stranger - so the community had a duty to care for the poor and to treat all people with charity, compassion and kindness.
The Romans - when war is just: Roman ethics was greatly influenced by the Stoics, who believed in the natural equality of all people and in living by the four cardinal virtues: wisdom, courage, justice and temperance. One moral issue that concerned the Romans was war. The orator Cicero (106-43 BCE), a Stoic, set out in his work De Officiis when war could be justified. He taught that the only cause for war was so that people might live unharmed in peace, and that a war without just cause is unjust. There should be no war without an official demand for satisfaction or a formal declaration after a proper warning. War could be fought to protect the safety of a city, protect the innocent, avenge wrongs and honour pledges to allies, and after victory mercy should be shown to the defeated. Cicero's teaching later influenced St Augustine in the early Church.

- The Romans: Cicero stated that wars undertaken without cause are unjust.

Choose two of the above religions and trace how a basic principle from their teaching could influence their members' understanding of what is right and wrong behaviour in a situation.

'Zakat' means purification and growth: possessions are purified by setting aside a percentage for those in need. Zakat of self is given before the end of Ramadan, and Zakat of wealth is given at the end of the year by those with surplus wealth. Muslims believe that all things belong to Allah and that those with wealth only hold it in trust. Situation: a Muslim family has had a good year in business while people in their town are homeless or struggling to buy food. Because of Zakat, they would understand that it is right to share their surplus with the poor - for example by donating money or food - and that hoarding wealth is wrong. Judaism - reverence for life: In Judaism, morality comes from the relationship with God, shaped by the Torah and the Covenant. The Decalogue (Ten Commandments) teaches 'You shall not kill', and reverence for life is one of the most distinctive Jewish values: life is sacred. Jewish teaching says a dying patient's end should not be hastened; the Talmud says that a person who shoots a man as he falls off a cliff is guilty of murder, even though the man would die anyway. So their understanding of right and wrong would lead them to protect life and to oppose euthanasia. In the same way, the principle that killing is wrong could lead Jewish people to oppose the death penalty.

prompt:
Explain how having an informed conscience could guide a person to behave in a morally mature way in a decision-making situation.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
An informed conscience is a conscience that a person has made an effort to educate, so that they learn in their hearts what is right and wrong. Without this, we may simply rely on our own feelings, which can be lazy or selfish. The key phrase is: 'We decide for ourselves, but we do not decide by ourselves.'
How it guides moral maturity: A morally mature person moves away from self-interest towards decisions based on values and principles. A morally immature person is often blocked by ignorance and bias, or simply follows the crowd: 'I thought it was wrong, but everyone is doing it.' An informed conscience helps to overcome this in three ways.
1. It looks at all the facts and consequences. Informing conscience means listening to what others have learnt before us and to people we respect. This makes a person aware of how their choice will affect others, so they act in a way that helps rather than harms.
2. It draws on wisdom beyond ourselves. A Christian informs their conscience by listening to the Word of God in scripture, taking part in the sacraments, listening to Church teaching, praying, and looking at the lives of good people. Virtue ethics also helps: using wisdom, courage, justice and balance to decide.
3. It leads to responsibility. A healthy conscience hears all the voices, but the final say is our own. Acting on conscience can take honesty and courage, and it means truly taking responsibility for our actions.
Situation: A family must decide whether to keep a seriously ill relative on a life-support machine. A person with an informed conscience would not decide on feelings alone. They would seek medical advice, reflect on the teaching of their faith, talk to people who have been in a similar situation, and think about what the person would want. Having listened to all of this, they would make a thoughtful decision based on love and respect for the person rather than on what is easiest for themselves, and take responsibility for it. Another example is someone offered a bribe to help a person get planning permission: an informed conscience leads them to say, 'I will follow my conscience and not take a bribe,' even though it costs them. In both cases the informed conscience guides the person to act in a mature, unselfish and responsible way.

- It guides a person to take responsibility for their actions.

prompt:
Imagine you are working in a group choosing a person who could be honoured for the part their ideas played in the development of philosophy.
Explain a reason why Socrates could be selected for the part any one of his ideas played in the development of philosophy.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
Socrates should be honoured for his idea of Socratic ignorance, because it taught philosophy to begin by questioning what we think we know.

Socrates was born in Athens around 470 BCE. He wrote nothing himself; we know him through his pupils Plato and Xenophon. He was a ceaseless questioner who said, 'The unexamined life is not worth living.'

At his trial he set himself apart from the Sophists, who claimed vast wisdom. Socrates said most people think they know more than they really do, and that his only wisdom was knowing how little he knew. He asked 'innocent' questions of so-called experts to expose the gaps in their reasoning and get nearer to the truth.

This idea shaped the whole development of philosophy. It showed that great thinkers must question their own assumptions before forming a theory. Plato built his dialogues on this method of questioning and argument. Much later, Rene Descartes used a 'method of doubt', doubting everything he could before building up certain knowledge. Even today, philosophy works by challenging preconceptions through reflection and argument. For that reason Socrates deserves the honour.

prompt:
From your knowledge of Socrates' thinking outline the points he might emphasise for people today on one of the following ideas:
- The moral good
- The importance of essence
(20 marks)
model_answer:
I will outline the points Socrates might make today about the moral good.

First, he would tell us to care for the soul above all. In his day Athenians cared for wealth, status and their bodies but neglected the soul. Today we can be just as focused on money, image and social media. Socrates would remind us that wealth, beauty or strength cannot create virtue, but virtue creates everything that is truly good for us.

Second, he would say that what pleases us is not necessarily good. Against the Sophists, who said the strongest argument wins, he taught that we must act for the common good. Today this could mean working on issues like housing or the cost-of-living crisis, not just looking after ourselves.

Third, he would stress that it is never right to do wrong, even when we have been wronged. Revenge is not justified.

Finally, he would say that true happiness comes from living well, not just living: 'The really important thing is not to live but to live well.' Pleasure is good, but lasting happiness only comes through a virtuous life.

prompt:
Describe two examples of how an interest in the spiritual can be seen in the lives of people who lived in an ancient society.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Example 1: Newgrange, County Meath
Newgrange is a Neolithic monument built around 3200 BCE. The mound was used for burial and for rituals connected with the winter solstice. It is astronomically aligned with the sun: on 21 December, the shortest day, the rising sun shines through the roof box above the entrance and lights up the inner chamber. After that date the days lengthen, so for the people the sun had returned and darkness was defeated. This may have given them hope at the darkest time of the year. The stones are covered in carved spirals and wavy lines, especially on the huge entrance stone. Some scholars think the spirals symbolise the cycle of life, death and rebirth; others think they stand for the sun, moon and stars. Either way, the builders wanted to be in harmony with the universe and to express a sense of something 'other', even sacred, at the centre of existence.

Example 2: Rites of passage
Ancient societies marked life's big changes - birth, puberty, marriage and death - with special rituals called rites of passage. Arnold van Gennep showed they follow a three-part pattern: separation, transition and incorporation. Among the Murngin people of northern Australia, a boy was told the Great Father Snake was calling him. Over many nights he was shown dances symbolising his ancestors and taught myths explaining the world. He was sent on a long journey, and finally circumcised, after which the tribe saw him as a man. Joseph Campbell said the boys were symbolically killed and reborn into adulthood. These rites show an early human need to understand the cosmos and to be in harmony with it - a clear sign of spiritual interest.

An excellent answer shows an understanding of spirituality by giving an account of two ways that an interest in the spiritual (self-transcendence through knowledge, love, religious experience) can be seen in the lives of people in a society from the very distant past. Points of reference, e.g.: the ancient ritual of burying the dead reflects an interest in the cycle of life, death and rebirth - the triple spiral carvings on the large kerbstones at Newgrange, Co. Meath; the myths of Prometheus and Gilgamesh are some of the earliest examples of how people communicated their interest in the spiritual; times of transition or change were marked by special rituals in ancient societies - rites of passage expressing the human need to be in harmony with the cosmos. prompt:

The quotation comes from John O'Donohue's book Anam Cara. Spirituality is about a person's inner being and the mysterious, 'other' side of life.
