There is strong evidence that interest in spirituality is growing, and it helps people search for meaning in at least two ways.

1. Meditation and mindfulness
Bookshops now have whole Spirituality sections on prayer and meditation, and there is great openness to Eastern practices such as meditation, yoga and mindfulness. In a noisy, busy world, people need silence and stillness. Meditation calms the mind so a person can reflect on who they are and what matters to them. For religious people it can also be a way to connect with God. Pope Francis said, 'We all need to meditate, to reflect, to find ourselves.' This shows how meditation helps the search for meaning.

Weekly Mass attendance in Ireland is falling, yet pilgrimages remain hugely popular. prompt:
The development of a secular value system can be traced back to particular points in time, such as how a focus on human rights followed the French Revolution, etc.
Describe two other examples, from different points in time, of how a secular value system developed.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Example 1: The Renaissance (15th and 16th centuries)
Secularism can be traced back to the Renaissance, a time of huge innovation in art, music, literature, architecture, philosophy and religion. It began in Italy and spread across Europe. Its most important development was humanism. Renaissance humanism was marked by individualism: it placed human beings at the centre and saw each person as unique, special and able to understand the world. It valued the power of reason above all else. This confidence in human potential led to great creativity, especially in science. Modern scientific discoveries can be traced back to the growth of scientific reasoning and secular humanism at this time. A key thinker was Desiderius Erasmus. This focus on the individual and on reason, rather than on Church authority, is still common in today's society and laid the foundation for a secular value system.

Example 2: Existentialism (20th century)
World War I (1914-1918) caused around twenty million deaths. Many in the next generation were disillusioned. They no longer looked to the Church for meaning and believed they had only themselves in the search for meaning. Existentialism grew from this. It starts with the individual as a free and responsible agent who decides their own development by free will. Jean-Paul Sartre said, 'Man is condemned to be free.' Each person must decide for or against an action and take full responsibility for it, without outside rules of right and wrong. Existentialism rejects any meaning from outside the person, such as religion. Its stress on the individual and on freedom made an important contribution to secular humanism and has had an enormous impact on the values of Western society today.

prompt:
- Essenes
- Pharisees
- Sadducees
Outline a similarity and a difference in the reaction of two Jewish groups listed above to Roman rule in Palestine at the time of Jesus of Nazareth.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
I will compare the Pharisees and the Sadducees.

Background: In 63 BCE the Romans took control of Palestine. Jews believed the land was a gift from God and a sign of the covenant, so being ruled by a pagan, polytheistic empire was a serious problem. Each Jewish group reacted differently.

Similarity
Both groups shared a history, belief in the one true God and the Law of Moses in the Torah, so neither welcomed rule by a foreign power that affected their religious life. Yet neither chose violent resistance like the Zealots. Both found a way to live under Rome without open rebellion and both had a place in the Jewish government structure: the Sadducees as the most powerful group, and the scribes and Pharisees as the experts on the Law. Rome wanted peace in the region, and neither group was a threat to it.

Difference
The Sadducees reacted by co-operating with Rome. They were mainly wealthy, powerful conservatives linked to the Temple. They had held power before the Romans came and kept it by working with the 'enemy', helping to run the puppet government that administered law and collected taxes. They followed the path of least resistance. The risk was a loss of Jewish identity, and they did not survive.
The Pharisees, by contrast, believed survival came only through strict observance of the Law of Moses and its rituals, such as keeping the Sabbath holy. This kept Jewish identity distinct from Greeks and Romans. They were free to follow the Law as long as they paid taxes. Unlike the Sadducees, they survived, because the Law was their means of survival.

prompt:
Describe two examples of how the teaching of Jesus of Nazareth is remembered by Christians today in one of the following ways:
- The search for Christian unity
- Rites of Christian worship
(40 marks)
model_answer:
I will describe how Jesus' teaching is remembered in rites of Christian worship.

Example 1: The Eucharist
At the Last Supper, a Passover meal, Jesus took bread and the cup and said, 'This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me' (Luke 22:19). The apostles kept this command, and Acts 2:42-47 describes the first Christians 'breaking bread' together. Christians today still celebrate the Eucharist. It has two parts: the Liturgy of the Word, where readings from scripture recall the words and actions of Jesus, and the Liturgy of the Eucharist. For Catholics, 'memorial' is at the heart of the eucharistic prayers - making a past event effective in the present - and Christ is truly present after the consecration. Protestants focus on remembering the last meal, with bread and wine as symbols of Christ's presence. This 're-membering' is also a call to live as Jesus did: 'you also ought to wash one another's feet' (John 13:14).

Example 2: Baptism
Baptism initiates a person into the Church, following Jesus' command to baptise all nations (Matthew 28). In the Catholic rite, the prayer before baptism recalls how Jesus overcame evil and brings freedom from original sin. The child is anointed with oil, recalling Christ 'our saviour'. The blessing of the water remembers the blood and water from Jesus' side. 'Baptise' means 'to plunge': going into the water symbolises being buried with Christ in his death and rising as 'a new creature'. It also reminds believers of Jesus' own baptism in the Jordan. Parents and godparents promise to raise the child in the faith, so the teaching of Jesus is passed on.

Movement 1: The Mendicant Orders (13th century)
In the 12th and 13th centuries many Christians saw the clergy as a powerful, wealthy group whose lifestyle did not match gospel values. The Mendicant ('begging') orders returned to the lifestyle of Jesus in the Gospels. This had a deep effect on their members. As individuals they owned nothing and had the right to beg, so they lived in real poverty like Jesus. Pastoral care became the focus of their training. St Francis of Assisi, son of a wealthy merchant, gave up his wealth for a life of poverty and preaching, and young men followed him to imitate Christ in all things; the Franciscans were especially effective in preaching to the poor. St Dominic founded a group committed to absolute poverty and preaching, the Order of Preachers. Importantly, the friars stayed within the Church and brought it new life, rather than breaking away.

Movement 2: Liberation Theology (1968 onwards)
Vatican II called the Church to read the signs of the times in the light of the gospel. In 1968 at Medellin, Colombia, Latin American bishops concluded that their society was unjust, with most people living in poverty and oppression. Returning to Jesus' concern for the poor, they made a 'preferential option for the poor'. Gustavo Gutierrez's A Theology of Liberation (1971) presented Jesus as the great liberator and the gospel as a message of freedom. The effect on members was that working for justice became truly following Jesus. They worked to transform society so all could live in dignity. This came at a cost: it upset the powerful, and some activists were tortured or killed, most famously Archbishop Oscar Romero in 1980.

prompt:
Describe a religious ceremony that marks the entry/initiation of a new member into one of the following religions:
- Buddhism
- Hinduism
- Islam
(20 marks)
model_answer:
I will describe Shin Byu, the Theravada Buddhist initiation ceremony.

Shin Byu is the coming-of-age ceremony for a boy of about twelve. It marks his full entry into Buddhism.

At the start, the boy is dressed in expensive clothes and a feast is held in his honour, a little like a prince. This recalls the life of the Buddha, who was born a prince before giving up his wealth.

Then an older monk removes the expensive clothes and replaces them with a simple saffron robe. The boy's head is shaved and he is given a begging bowl. These actions show that he is turning away from luxury and worldly things, just as the Buddha did.

Next he takes the vow of the Three Jewels (the Three Refuges): 'I go to the Buddha for refuge. I go to the Dharma for refuge. I go to the Sangha for refuge.' This commits him to the Buddha, his teaching and the community of monks.

Finally he enters the monastery and lives as a monk for one night, one week or even years. After this he is a fully initiated Buddhist.

prompt:

- A New Religious Movement
- Baha'i Faith
- Chinese Religion

model_answer:
I will compare Christianity, a major world religion, with the Sikh religion.

Similarity: service to others
Both religions put serving others at the heart of daily practice. Christians follow Jesus' command of love: 'You shall love your neighbour as yourself.' At the Last Supper Jesus washed his disciples' feet as an example of unconditional love, and Christians today try to follow this by caring for the poor, for example through Trocaire or St Vincent de Paul. Sikhs practise seva: service to others, physical, mental and material, without expecting any reward. Sikhs see seva as a true form of worship. One of their three key duties is vand chhakna - to practise charity. Every gurdwara has a langar, a kitchen where free communal meals are prepared and shared with everyone. So in both religions, faith is lived out through practical goodness towards others.

Difference: religious leaders and identity
Many Christian churches have an ordained clergy. In the Catholic Church, Holy Orders is one of the seven sacraments, and priests lead the celebration of the Eucharist. Sikhism has no ordained priesthood and no monks or nuns. Any suitably educated Sikh may lead worship in the gurdwara, and all members of the Sangat are equal. Guru Nanak even rejected the monastic life as a path to spiritual growth.
There is also a difference in dress. Christianity has no universal religious dress for lay people. Members of the Sikh Khalsa wear the five Ks - kesh (uncut hair), kangha (comb), kara (metal bangle), kirpan (sword) and kachla (shorts) - as visible signs of their identity and commitment.

prompt:
Describe two examples of how the sense of awe and mystery associated with the 'sacred' can be communicated through individual people within a religion.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Rudolf Otto said the experience of the holy is central to religion. It is mysterious, cannot be described literally, and brings out feelings of awe and humility. Holy people are those who speak on God's behalf or mediate between people and God, and so they can pass this sense of awe on to others.

Example 1: The shaman in primal religion
A shaman is a tribal elder or holy person who is a living mediator between the human world and the spirit world. Shamanism began with the Tungus people of Siberia and north-east China. The shaman usually inherits the gift from his or her ancestors and builds a close relationship with a spiritual guardian through fasting and prayer. Through sacred trances the shaman journeys into the spirit world to gain prophetic wisdom and knowledge of healing. Using charms, chants and sacrifices, the shaman interprets the will of the gods and cures disease. The shaman is said to be 'seized by the Divine' - controlling the spirits yet possessed by them. To the community, the shaman makes the mysterious spirit world present, and people approach him or her with awe and respect.

Example 2: Moses in Judaism
In Exodus 3, God called to Moses out of a burning bush: 'Come no closer! Remove the sandals from your feet, for the place on which you are standing is holy ground.' Moses hid his face, because he was afraid to look at God. This shows the experience of the holy - awe, fear, humility, and ground set apart. Moses then became God's messenger, sent to lead the Israelites out of Egypt. Through him the people came to know the God of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob. In this way one individual's experience of the sacred was communicated to a whole people, and it is still remembered with reverence today.

prompt:

model_answer:
All of Jesus' moral teaching is summed up in one command: love God and love your neighbour. When asked which commandment was first, he answered, 'You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart... You shall love your neighbour as yourself' (Mark 12:28-34). This love is agape - unselfish love that seeks only the good of the other. Right relationship means living justly with God, our neighbour and the world.

Jesus would remind young Christians that people come first. He said, 'The Sabbath was made for humankind, not humankind for the Sabbath.' He went out of his way to be with the poor, the sick and outsiders. In the parable of the Good Samaritan, the hero is a Samaritan - a man the Jews despised - who helps a wounded Jew, while the priest and Levite pass by. Today Jesus might ask us to include people who are left out: someone new in school, a person of a different background, or migrants and refugees. He would also warn against self-righteousness: only the humble see God's grace at work.

Point 2: Be people of peace and forgiveness
In the Sermon on the Mount Jesus said, 'Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you,' and 'turn the other cheek.' This is not weakness: it means facing hurt with dignity and strength rather than revenge, so a new relationship can begin. Jesus lived this when he forgave those who crucified him. prompt:
Examine how a balance between 'the common good' and 'individual rights' is encouraged in two examples of Irish civil law.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The common good is what is best for the whole of society, shared by all and sought for the fulfilment of all. In 1937 Eamon de Valera said the law must ensure that 'the rights of the individual... and the rights of a community... do not conflict and properly coordinate.' Personal rights are protected in Articles 40-44 of the Constitution, but they are not absolute: they are balanced with the common good.

Example 1: Road traffic law
Hundreds of people die in car accidents in Ireland each year, yet the State does not ban driving, because people have a right to travel and banning cars would harm society's progress. Instead, the law gives individuals the right to own and drive a car, but limits that right with speed limits and drink-driving limits. These rules protect the common good by preventing dangerous driving that would put other people's lives at risk. The Church also names neglecting speed limits as a block to the common good. So the law protects both freedom to drive and the safety of everyone.

Example 2: The Murray case
Noel and Marie Murray were serving life sentences for the murder of a Garda. They argued that under the Constitution they had a right to marry and have children, so they should be allowed conjugal visits in prison. The Supreme Court held that this right was subservient to the common good of the community, which must be protected from dangerous criminals. Prisoners lose some rights, such as the right to vote, and marriage rights depend on a person being free to carry them out. They lost the case.

Both examples show that Irish law respects individual rights, but when they clash with the safety of society, the common good can be given greater weight.

prompt:
Name a moral theorist and describe what is involved in two stages of moral development they suggest a person might go through before reaching moral maturity.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The moral theorist I have chosen is Lawrence Kohlberg. He applied Jean Piaget's developmental approach to morality and was also influenced by Immanuel Kant. He gave children moral dilemmas and asked them to judge the conflict. He concluded that people pass through three levels, each with two stages - six stages in all. Each stage builds on the one before, and you cannot skip a stage. For Kohlberg the morally mature person is at the post-conventional level, guided by principles and conscience. Before that, a person goes through the following stages.

Stage 1: Obedience-Punishment Orientation (Pre-conventional level, about age 4-10)
At the pre-conventional level, moral value lies in a person's own needs and wants. In Stage 1, moral judgement is driven by the need to avoid punishment. Right and wrong are judged by the consequences for me. For example, little Hugh will not hit his sister because he does not want to get shouted at. He is not thinking about his sister's feelings, only about the punishment. Adults can still act at this stage, for example a soldier who carries out an atrocity in war to avoid being killed.

Stage 3: 'Good Boy/Nice Girl' Orientation (Conventional level, about age 10-13)
At the conventional level, moral value lies in keeping the conventional order and pleasing others. In Stage 3, moral judgement is driven by the need to avoid disapproval from others. For example, Hugh will not disturb his Maths class because the teacher will get a bad impression of him. This stage can be summed up as conformity: 'Everyone is doing it, so it must be okay.' The big 'sin' is to be different. This is a step forward because the person now thinks about others, but they are still not acting from their own principles.

prompt:
Outline one philosophical idea put forward by the Sophists in ancient Greece.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
One key idea of the Sophists was relativism: the view that there is no absolute or objective truth.

The Sophists were travelling teachers in fifth-century Athens. Athens was a democracy, and to succeed in public life you needed to speak well, so wealthy young men paid the Sophists to train them, especially in rhetoric (the use of language to persuade). The Sophists were not seekers of truth. They taught students to argue both sides of a case equally fiercely, whether they agreed or not, simply to win.

Behind this was their belief that truth is relative. Protagoras said, 'Man is the measure of all things.' This means each person decides what is true and good for them. Protagoras and Gorgias gave the example of two people: one says it is hot, the other says it is not - and for the Sophists both are true. Gorgias added that there is no way to tell knowledge from opinion, because we filter everything through our own thoughts and words.

So for the Sophists, what is morally right depended on the individual or the culture, not on any universal standard. Truth became closer to opinion than fact. Thrasymachus even claimed that 'justice is nothing else than the interest of the stronger.'

Other valid ideas accepted. Graded on four criteria: evidence of the marking criteria, relevance, use of skill, factual accuracy. prompt:
Assess the impact of one idea put forward by the Sophists in ancient Greece on the development of philosophy.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
The Sophists' idea of relativism - Protagoras' claim that 'Man is the measure of all things' - had a large impact on philosophy, partly because it put people at the centre and partly because others reacted so strongly against it.

First, it changed the focus of philosophy. Earlier thinkers like Thales and Heraclitus asked about the natural world: how the universe began and what it is made of. By saying the human person is the measure of truth, the Sophists shifted attention to people and their place in the world. Later philosophers kept human experience at the centre, which was a crucial step for philosophy and later for humanism.

Second, it provoked a strong reply. Socrates, Plato and Aristotle all criticised the Sophists. Socrates searched for a universal definition of justice against Sophist relativism, and used critical questioning instead of clever rhetoric to reach real knowledge. Aristotle's idea of an ordered universe set in motion by an intelligent being was also a rejection of relativism.

On balance, the impact was significant but often negative: much of the greatest Greek philosophy was built as an answer to the Sophists. Their questioning, sceptical attitude was valuable, yet today 'sophist' means someone who argues to win without believing what they say.

prompt:
Christianity / Islam / Judaism
Examine how the understanding of God in one of the above religions could influence a person's belief about their purpose in life in the world today.

I will examine the Christian understanding of God.

Christians believe in one God who is beyond full human understanding, yet who wants to be known as loving and caring, the creator and sustainer of all. The First Letter of John says simply, 'God is love' (1 John 4:8). If a person believes they were created by a God of love, they may believe their life has meaning and that they are valued. Their purpose is to love God in return and to share that love with others.

Christians believe God revealed himself most fully in Jesus: God became flesh, and Jesus' life, death and resurrection are a saving event. This could influence a Christian today to see their purpose as following Jesus' example - his care for the poor, his forgiveness and his service - and spreading his message. Because the resurrection offers salvation and eternal life, a Christian may see life as a journey towards God, not something that ends at death. This can give hope in hard times.

Christians also believe God is a Trinity - Father, Son and Holy Spirit - one God in three persons, formalised at the Council of Nicaea in 325. The Trinity is a community of love. This could lead a Christian to believe their purpose is to live in loving community with others, not in isolation.

Finally, God is personal, forgiving and merciful. Jesus called God 'Abba', an intimate word like 'dad'. A person who sees God this way may believe they are called into a close relationship with God through prayer, and that even after failure they can begin again. After the ascension God continues to act through the Holy Spirit, so a Christian may feel guided and strengthened in their daily choices.

In today's busy, materialistic world, this understanding of God can give a person a clear purpose: to love God and neighbour, to follow Jesus, and to work towards eternal life with God.

prompt:
Agnosticism / Atheism / Reductionism
Choose two of the above viewpoints and explain how a person's religious faith could be challenged by each of the points of view you have chosen.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Atheism
Atheism is the denial of the existence of God. Some people choose it deliberately; others simply cannot believe religious teachings. Theoretical atheism is based on ideas that seem to make belief impossible. One example is the problem of evil and suffering: if God is all-loving and all-powerful, why does he allow innocent people to suffer? A believer who faces a tragedy, such as the death of a child, could find this question very hard and begin to doubt whether a loving God exists. Another example is the claim that science and religion are incompatible. Militant atheism goes further and argues that religious belief is harmful and restricts human potential. Hearing this could make a person of faith feel their beliefs are foolish or damaging, and so shake their faith.

Agnosticism
Agnosticism holds that we can only know what can be seen and understood using reason and science. The term was first used in 1876 by the biologist Thomas Henry Huxley, a supporter of Darwin, who believed the question of a higher power is unsolved and insoluble. Today an agnostic is someone who thinks the evidence for or against God is inconclusive. Strict agnostics say we can never know; empirical agnostics say we do not know yet. This could challenge a person's faith by highlighting uncertainty. A believer may start to ask, 'How can I be sure?' Because there is no scientific proof that God exists, they may feel their faith has no firm basis. Agnosticism is a form of scepticism, which questions whether humans can know the truth at all, so it could lead a believer to doubt the truth of their religion's teachings.

Both viewpoints, then, ask the person of faith to justify their belief and may lead them to doubt, or to think more deeply about why they believe.

prompt:
Outline two images of God that you have studied.
(20 marks)
model_answer:
God as Father
This is a traditional image. Jesus called God his father, using the intimate word 'Abba'. In the prayer Jesus taught his disciples he began, 'Father, hallowed be your name' (Luke 11:1-4). The image shows God caring for humanity as a parent cares for a child - protecting and guiding them. It is a familiar image, but it is only one part of God's identity, which can never be fully known. It appears in art such as God the Father by Luca Cambiaso.

God as Liberator

prompt:
Explain the new understanding of Jesus that developed among his disciples because of each of the following:
- The death of Jesus
- The Resurrection of Jesus
(40 marks)
model_answer:
The death of Jesus
At first the death of Jesus was deeply shocking for his followers. Crucifixion was the most humiliating and cruel Roman punishment, used for the lowest criminals. They were left without their leader; some ran away in terror and some may have lost hope and gone home. Many had hoped he would be a Messiah who would free them from Roman rule.

Later, however, they came to see his death in a new way. Paul hands on the early belief that 'Christ died for our sins in accordance with the scriptures' (1 Corinthians 15:3). They understood his death as fulfilling the prophecies about a suffering Messiah, such as Isaiah's suffering servant, and Jesus himself had said the Son of Man must suffer and be killed (Mark 8:31). At the Last Supper he had offered himself in a new covenant between God and the people. They now saw his death as a ransom - the price paid for humanity's freedom from sin and death. Jesus was the Redeemer and the mediator of salvation, through whom all people are reconciled to God.

The Resurrection of Jesus
The empty tomb and the appearances - to Mary Magdalene, to Peter, to the twelve and to more than five hundred people - forced the disciples to see that Jesus was more than they had imagined. Only now did they really understand who he was. The Resurrection confirmed him as the Messiah and the Son of God, and showed that God approved his life and teaching. They came to see that God had been revealed in Jesus, the mystery of the Incarnation: 'Whoever has seen me has seen the Father' (John 14:9). New titles emerged: the fish symbol stood for 'Jesus Christ, Son of God, Saviour', and 'Jesus is Lord' sums up their belief. They were transformed, gained a sense of mission (Matthew 28:19), and after Pentecost acted together to continue his work.

prompt:
Discuss the reliability of the key points of evidence for Jesus of Nazareth put forward by any two of the following sources:
- Josephus
- Pliny the Younger
- Saint Paul
- Tacitus
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Tacitus
Tacitus (c. 56-117 CE) was a Roman historian writing around 115 CE. He refers to Jesus when describing the burning of Rome in 64 CE, which Emperor Nero blamed on the Christians. He writes that 'Christus, the founder of the name, had undergone the death penalty in the reign of Tiberius, by sentence of... Pontius Pilate', and that this 'pernicious superstition' broke out again in Judea and then in Rome itself.

Key points: Jesus existed, he was executed under Pontius Pilate during Tiberius' reign, and Christianity spread from Judea to Rome. This evidence is considered reliable because Tacitus was hostile to Christians - he had no reason to invent Jesus. However, he wrote about eighty years after the crucifixion, so he is a secondary source, and not all historians accept his account of Nero's cruelty.

Josephus
Flavius Josephus (c. 37-100 CE) was a Jewish historian. He fought against Rome in the Jewish rebellion, surrendered to Vespasian, and later worked within the circle of the emperors Vespasian and Titus. In The Jewish Antiquities he mentions Jesus in the context of Jewish disturbances under Pontius Pilate. He describes Jesus as 'a wise man, a doer of wonderful works, a teacher of men who receive the truth with pleasure'.

Key points: Jesus was a real person, a teacher and wonder-worker, who had a deep and lasting impact on the people he met. His evidence is considered reliable because he was not a follower of Jesus, so he was not writing to promote Christian faith. On the other hand, he wrote about sixty years after the crucifixion, so he was not an eyewitness.

Conclusion: neither source is a primary source, but this is normal in ancient history - there are none for Socrates either. Because both writers were non-Christians, and Tacitus was openly hostile, together they give strong, authoritative evidence that Jesus really lived and was crucified.

Points of reference: Josephus - a Jewish historian working for the Romans, refers to Jesus as a wise man, a doer of wonderful works, who was crucified under Pilate, and says his followers continued after his death; considered reliable since he was not a follower of Jesus. Pliny the Younger - in his letter to Emperor Trajan writes about early Christians worshipping Jesus as a God; though he doesn't detail Jesus' life he highlights Jesus' importance; considered reliable as a non-Christian historical source. St Paul - emphasised Jesus' death and resurrection as central to Christian faith and claimed to have encountered the risen Jesus; Paul did not know the historical Jesus and writes from a faith-based perspective. Tacitus - a Roman historian who mentioned 'Christus' being executed under Tiberius and blames Christians for the great fire of Rome; his negative view of Christians adds reliability, confirming Jesus' historical existence and death. prompt:
Describe how the way of life of members of one of the early Christian communities listed below was influenced by the teaching of Jesus that all people are equal and welcome in the Kingdom of God:
- Corinth
- Philippi
- Thessalonica
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Philippi was a city of great importance in the Roman province of Macedonia, in north-eastern Greece, home to Greeks, Macedonians and a small number of Jews. The Christian community there was founded by Paul and Silas around 49 or 50 CE on Paul's second missionary journey. It is believed to be the first Christian community in Europe.

Welcoming everyone: The Acts of the Apostles tells how Paul and Silas met a woman named Lydia, who was baptised with her whole family. Others were impressed and the Church at Philippi grew. This shows Jesus' teaching that all are welcome: a woman and her household were among the very first members, and most members were Gentiles (non-Jews).

Gentiles as equal members: Some Jewish Christian missionaries urged the Philippians to keep Jewish laws such as circumcision. Paul assured them that keeping Jewish law was not required for membership, and explained in his letter that circumcision was not needed for non-Jews. Gentiles were welcomed as full and equal members, just as Jesus welcomed outsiders into the Kingdom.

Caring and sharing: Believers met in small groups for prayer, preaching and the breaking of bread. They cared for the weak and needy among them, and their generosity even extended to supporting Paul on his journeys. This selfless love and mutual service lived out Jesus' message of love of God and neighbour - no one was left out because they were poor or weak. The community was known as enthusiastic, joyful and generous.

Unity: When two prominent women, Euodia and Syntyche, quarrelled, Paul warned of the dangers of internal conflict and urged them to unite as members of one Church with one goal. Equality in the Kingdom meant living as one family.

Even when they faced persecution from non-believing Gentiles, the Philippians tried to live as a community where everyone belonged.

prompt:
Trace an example of how inter-faith dialogue developed between members of two of the following religions:
- Buddhism
- Christianity
- Hinduism
- Islam
- Judaism
(40 marks)
model_answer:
I will trace the development of dialogue between Christianity and Judaism.

A painful starting point: Christianity grew out of Judaism. Jesus was a Jew, most of the first Christians were Jewish, and both share the Hebrew Bible and belief in one creator God. Yet for centuries there was anti-Semitism (hostility to Jews), often started or ignored by the Church, which left deep hurt.

First steps: In the twentieth century attitudes began to change. Pope Pius XI declared, 'We are all spiritually Semites.' In 1960 Pope John XXIII greeted Jewish visitors with the words, 'I am Joseph, your brother.'

Vatican II: The Second Vatican Council's document Nostra Aetate was a turning point. It stated that 'the Catholic Church rejects nothing in those religions which is true and holy' and that they 'often reflect a ray of that Truth which enlightens all human beings.' It recognised the Jewish people as brothers and affirmed God's ongoing covenant with them, opening the way for respectful dialogue.

Further developments: In 1980 the German Bishops said that anti-Semitism is ultimately against Christ himself. In 1986 Pope John Paul II visited the synagogue in Rome and called Jews 'our beloved elder brothers'. He also asked forgiveness for the wrongs done to Jews, and in 2000, at Yad Vashem, the Holocaust memorial in Jerusalem, he said: 'We wish to remember... to ensure that never again will evil prevail.'

Dialogue today: Groups such as the Council of Christians and Jews foster ongoing dialogue, and the Sisters of Sion are a religious order working for Jewish-Christian reconciliation.

So the relationship has developed from hostility and suspicion to one of mutual respect, co-operation and reconciliation - the qualities that real inter-faith dialogue needs.

prompt:
Describe the religious ceremonies used by two of the following religions to mark an important moment in their founding stories:
- Buddhism
- Christianity
- Hinduism
- Islam
- Judaism
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Judaism - Passover (Pesach)
Passover celebrates a key moment in the founding story of the Jewish people: God freeing the Israelites from slavery in Egypt, led by Moses (the Exodus). It is one of the three major 'foot' festivals and lasts eight days in spring. It is also called the Feast of Unleavened Bread.

The central ceremony is the Seder, a special meal held at home. During the meal the Haggadah, the story of the Exodus, is read aloud so that each generation remembers what God did. Children take an active part, asking, 'Why is this night different from all other nights?' Symbolic foods recall parts of the story. The most important is matzah, unleavened bread, which reminds Jews that their ancestors left Egypt in a hurry, with no time for the bread to rise.

Christianity - Easter
Easter celebrates the most important moment in the Christian story: the death and resurrection of Jesus. It is the most important festival of the year for all Christians - a festival of triumph over sin and death.

It is prepared for by Lent, seven weeks of penance and fasting, which ends with Holy Week. During Holy Week solemn rituals of service, mourning and penance recall the last events of Jesus' life: the Last Supper, his arrest in the Garden of Gethsemane, his trial and crucifixion. On Holy Saturday night the Easter Vigil is held. It is rich in symbols: the paschal (Easter) candle is lit in the darkness to show that Christ, the Light, has overcome the darkness of sin and death. The Vigil includes prayer, ritual and the Eucharist, and Easter Sunday is celebrated with great joy that Jesus is risen.

prompt:
Compare how the community of believers is structured in two of the following religions:
- Buddhism
- Christianity
- Hinduism
- Islam
- Judaism
(40 marks)
model_answer:
I will compare Christianity and Islam.

Christianity: Christianity is like a tree with many branches. Its three main branches are Roman Catholicism, Eastern Orthodoxy and Protestantism, plus many Pentecostal/Evangelical churches. Each has strong structures of ministry and authority. The Roman Catholic Church is hierarchical: it is headed by the Pope, the successor of St Peter, with bishops worldwide as successors of the apostles, and only celibate men may be priests and bishops. Orthodox priests may marry. Protestant churches reject the authority of the Pope, and some, like the Anglican Communion, ordain women. Christians find authority in scripture, tradition and the ordained hierarchy.

Islam: Muslims belong to the Umma, the worldwide community of Muslims. There is no priesthood in Islam and no distinctions based on race, colour or class. Authority lies in the Qur'an and the Sharia (Islamic law), which organise every part of life. The Ulama, scholars trained in Islamic law, interpret the Sharia and guide the community. There are divisions: Sunni Muslims (about 90 per cent) believe the caliph should be elected; Shia Muslims believe the imam must be a descendant of Muhammad through Ali. Sufis are a smaller group of mystics.

Similarities: Both are worldwide communities united by one faith despite many divisions. In both, scripture is a key source of authority, and both have leaders who guide believers - bishops and ministers in Christianity, scholars and imams in Islam.

Differences: The biggest difference is priesthood and hierarchy. Catholic Christianity has a clear chain of authority from the Pope down, and priests who celebrate sacraments; Islam has no priests and no single head, with authority resting in the Sharia itself. Also, Christian divisions often arose over teaching and authority (e.g. Protestants rejecting the Pope), while the main divisions in Islam arose over leadership of the community, not doctrine.

An excellent answer gives an accurate account of similarities and/or differences in the way the community of members in two religions listed is arranged and organised. prompt:
Explain how a balance between personal and communal values can be seen in one example of a secular moral code you have studied.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
A secular moral code is a set of values and rules that does not depend on religion. One example is the Irish Constitution (1937), which sets out the rights of citizens and the duties of the State.

Personal values: Personal values are qualities an individual sees as good and important, such as freedom. The Constitution protects personal, or fundamental, rights in Articles 40 to 44 - for example the right to marry and have a family. These protect each person's dignity and freedom.

Communal values: Communal values seek the good of the whole community. For example, the State values the right of all to an education and pledges to protect it. When the Constitution was debated in the Dáil in 1937, Eamon de Valera said the law must make sure that 'the rights of the individual, as an individual, and the rights of a community, as a community, do not conflict and properly coordinate.'

How the balance works: Personal rights in the Constitution are not absolute; they are balanced with the common good. The courts show this balance in practice:
- The Derrynaflan Hoard: a priceless eighth-century chalice was found in 1980 by people who were trespassing. The court decided that the State's right to own national treasure, for the good of all, was a higher value than the finders' rights - though they were still given £25,000 as a gesture of good will.
- Noel and Marie Murray: serving life sentences for murdering a Garda, they claimed their constitutional right to marry and have children meant they should have conjugal visits. The Supreme Court ruled this right was subservient to the community's right to be protected from dangerous criminals.

Why balance is needed: The Supreme Court said in 1940 that the dignity and freedom of the individual cannot be achieved 'unless the social order is maintained'. So the personal good and the common good depend on each other. The same balance appears in everyday law: people are free to earn as much as they can, but must pay taxes so services can be provided for all.

In this way the Constitution avoids both extremes - individualism, which ignores others, and totalitarianism, which crushes the person for the State.

An excellent answer shows an understanding of the importance of personal and communal values by giving reasons as to how personal values are weighed against values that promote the good of all in the community in an example of a secular moral code. Points of reference, e.g.: Universal Declaration of Human Rights - balances personal rights (e.g. freedom of speech, freedom of religion) with communal values such as duties to the community for the general welfare of all; United States Constitution - protects personal freedoms (e.g. freedom of religion) while ensuring communal governance, such as equality under law of people of all religions. Bands (40 marks): Excellent 40-34, Very good 33-28, Good 27-22, Fair 21-16, Weak 15-10, Poor 9-0.

prompt:
Deontological Ethics / Hedonism / Modern Perspectives on Natural Law / Right Relationship / Teleological Ethics / Utilitarianism / Virtue Ethics
Outline the approach to deciding what is right and wrong put forward in two of the above moral theories.
(40 marks)
model_answer:
Deontological Ethics
The word comes from the Greek deon, meaning duty or obligation. Deontological ethics says there is an objective moral law - a code of behaviour that does not change over time or with the situation - which tells us how we should act. An action is judged not by its consequences but by whether it is right or wrong according to that law. The person deciding asks: 'What is the law? What is my duty?' For example, a deontologist would not break a red traffic light, even in the middle of the night with no one around, because it is against the law. They might say, 'I pay my taxes because it is my duty and the law demands it.' For a Christian, the moral law is inspired by the Word of God, so it is their duty to follow the Ten Commandments and the moral teachings of Jesus.

Teleological Ethics
The word comes from the Greek telos, meaning end or goal. Teleological ethics judges what is right by looking at the result of an action. Good actions are those that lead towards our fulfilment and ultimate happiness; the key question is 'What will happen as a result of my action?' and 'What good will be achieved?' For example, a teleologist might say, 'I pay my taxes because I want a fair opportunity in life for everyone,' or 'I do not smoke because it will damage my health and slow me down in sport.' For a Christian, the ultimate goal of life is to be with God, so an act is good if it leads towards that goal and evil if it stops a person reaching it.

In short, deontology focuses on duty and law, while teleology focuses on outcomes and goals.

prompt:
Compare the understanding of moral failure found in one Christian denomination with how it is understood in one of the following religions:
- Buddhism
- Hinduism
- Islam
- Judaism
(40 marks)
model_answer:
I will compare the Roman Catholic Church and Islam.

The Catholic Church: The Catechism defines sin as an offence against God: it 'sets itself against God's love for us and turns our hearts away from it' (CCC 1850). Sin breaks our relationship with God and neighbour and wounds the community. The Church distinguishes mortal sin - grave matter, committed with full knowledge and deliberate consent, which destroys love and turns a person away from God - from venial sin, which is less serious. It also speaks of original sin, a wound in our nature, and of social and structural sin, such as apartheid. The key response is forgiveness and reconciliation: Jesus died so that all might be free from sin, and Catholics celebrate God's forgiveness in the sacrament of Reconciliation, through confession, penance and absolution.

Islam: In Islam moral failure is mainly a religious concept: going against the will of Allah, revealed in the Qur'an. The greatest sin is shirk - calling any other god the true God. Each person is free to obey or disobey. Islam sees no need for a saviour; the way to salvation is through obedience, practising the Five Pillars and following Muhammad's example. On the Day of Judgement those whose good deeds outnumber their evil deeds will reach paradise.

Similarities: Both see moral failure as turning away from God's will. Both believe in life after death, judgement of sins, heaven and hell. Shirk is similar to breaking the first commandment. Both have a scripture and detailed rules - the Sharia is similar to the Church's medieval manuals for confessors.

Differences: Catholics believe in a saviour, Jesus, whose death brings forgiveness; Islam has no need for a saviour. Catholicism stresses a loving, personal covenant relationship with God, so sin damages a relationship and reconciliation restores it through a sacrament. In Islam (except the Sufi tradition) there is no such covenant relationship; obedience is the main virtue. Finally, Catholic teaching on sin comes from the unified authority of Church leaders, while in Islam authority lies in the Sharia, with no hierarchy.
